articles.title: BBC Inside Science - The future of mathematics in the age of AI - BBC Sounds
articles.summary: What next for the world of maths after a major intrusion by AI?
articles.body: Tom Whipple investigates one of the biggest days in the 10,000 year history of maths. This week, overnight, OpenAI dropped hundreds of mathematical papers onto the internet. From the Margulis-Platonov conjecture to the Gaussian Propeller conjecture to Banach’s simple Lebesgue-spectrum problem. Decades of maths progress overnight. PhDs of work done in hours. This week saw the Nobel Prizes awarded for Chemistry, Physics and Physiology or Medicine. From mice with blue lights in their brain to massive ice cubes with blue lights underground, science journalists Kit Chapman and Caroline Steel tell us what we need to know. In 2016, President Obama reflected on the moon landings and on the delicate and dangerous task of putting humans there. He commented, when giving a former MIT programmer the Presidential Medal of Freedom: “Our astronauts didn’t have much time...but thankfully they had Margaret Hamilton.” Margaret led the programming team for the Apollo missions and was a pioneer, in every sense of the word, until her death this week. Between Cape Horn and the Cape of Good Hope, there is a volcano inhabited by Chinstrap penguins. People don’t visit Zavodvski island much, but if you had been there in 2011 you would have been outnumbered by chinstraps 600,000 to one. Today, almost half a million have gone missing. Professor Norman Ratcliffe from the British Antarctic Survey tells us what he thinks is going on. Presenter: Tom Whipple Producers: Ben Mitchell, Clare Salisbury, Katie Tomsett Editor: Martin Smith Production Co-ordinator: Jana Bennett-Holesworth

articles.title: 5 Live Sport: All About... - The price of our sport - are fans being priced out? - BBC Sounds
articles.summary: Katie Smith is joined by Wake Up to Money’s Sean Farrington
articles.body:
Radio 5 Live , · 08 Oct 2026 , · 82 mins

Katie Smith is joined by Wake Up to Money's Sean Farrington and sport finance expert Dr Tom Bason to discuss the rising cost of tickets for major sporting events and subscription costs and ask why this is all happening and what might happen next? A range of guests join the pod including Richard Flint, chairman at Seat Unique - he comes on to discuss how the demand for live events has changed and they speak to psychologist Dr Kayleigh Smith about how the connection between fans and live sport has changed since the pandemic. There’s an interview with Mark Darbon from the R&A - about what it costs to put on a major sporting event, and how they aim to make things affordable. And not only that - Pete Oliver, DAZN’s CEO of growth markets joins the pod - to focus on how a newer streaming service approaches the market, and they will hear the impact from sport fans too.

articles.title: EUA terão primeira execução pública em 90 anos, diz site | G1
articles.standfirst: Nidal Hasan, condenado por matar 13 pessoas em ataque a tiros em uma base militar no Texas, será executado por fuzilamento em dezembro, segundo declaração do secretário de Defesa.
articles.summary: Nidal Hasan, condenado por matar 13 pessoas em ataque a tiros em Fort Hood, será executado por fuzilamento. Público poderá acompanhar a execução, diz secretário de Defesa.
articles.body:
Imagem de Hasan divulgada pelas autoridades em 2012 — Foto: Bell County Sheriff's Office/Reuters

O secretário de Defesa dos Estados Unidos , Pete Hegseth, afirmou nesta quinta-feira (8) que o público poderá assistir à execução de Nidal Hasan , condenado por matar 13 pessoas em um ataque a tiros na base militar de Fort Hood, no Texas, em 2009. A aplicação da pena está marcada para 3 de dezembro e será realizada por um pelotão de fuzilamento .

Em entrevista ao canal de TV Real America's Voice, Hegseth disse que o exército vai garantir que as pessoas possam acompanhar a execução. Segundo ele, a exposição pública serviria para mostrar que crimes deste tipo têm consequências graves nos EUA.

Ainda não está claro se haverá espectadores no local ou se a execução será transmitida pela internet ou pela televisão.

Questionado sobre se Hasan havia feito algum pedido final ou entrado em contato com o governo Trump, Hegseth respondeu apenas:

“Não me importa. Vamos vê-lo em 3 de dezembro.”

O porta-voz do Pentágono, Sean Parnell, havia dito na última segunda (5) que o presidente Donald Trump havia autorizado a execução de Hasan.

A última execução pública no país ocorreu em 1936, no Kentucky. Na ocasião, Rainey Bethea, um homem negro condenado por estuprar uma mulher branca, foi enforcado diante de uma multidão.

O caso marcaria o primeiro fuzilamento militar nos Estados Unidos desde 1945. O último aconteceu com o solado Eddie Slovik, morto na França por deserção durante a Segunda Guerra Mundial, segundo a emissora NPR.

A última execução de um militar dos Estados Unidos ocorreu em 1961, quando John A. Bennett foi enforcado no Kansas, após ser condenado por estupro e tentativa de assassinato de uma menina de 11 anos.

O fuzilamento é um método raro de execução no país. Apenas cinco estados — Idaho, Mississippi, Oklahoma, Carolina do Sul e Utah — autorizam essa prática, de acordo com o Centro de Informações sobre a Pena de Morte.

Em 2025, a Carolina do Sul realizou sua primeira execução por fuzilamento. Foi a primeira vez em 15 anos que o método foi usado nos Estados Unidos.

articles.title: How much worse can Yemen’s humanitarian crisis become?
articles.summary: UN says fighting has displaced more than 200,000 people in five weeks.
articles.body:
For more than a decade, Yemen has been facing one of the most severe humanitarian crises in the world.

The latest round of fighting between the government and the Houthis is worsening the suffering of millions of people.

articles.title: BYD diz que geopolítica é maior desafio para expansão | G1
articles.standfirst: Stella Li disse que a falta de previsibilidade nas relações internacionais dificulta investimentos e a entrada da montadora em novos mercados.
articles.summary: Stella Li disse que a falta de previsibilidade nas relações internacionais dificulta investimentos e a entrada da montadora em novos mercados.
articles.body:
Stella Li, responsável pelo negócio internacional da BYD, apresenta o caminhão elétrico ETT 44 durante feira em Hanover, na Alemanha. — Foto: REUTERS/Ilona Wissenbach

O principal desafio à expansão da BYD é a geopolítica , afirmou Stella Li, vice-presidente executiva da BYD , nesta quinta-feira (08), meses depois que o presidente da empresa chinesa declarou que a meta é se tornar a maior montadora do mundo em cinco anos.

“Quando fazemos negócios, queremos agir com certeza e visibilidade para que possamos controlar a situação e, assim, investir. Mas, com a geopolítica, nunca se sabe qual é a intenção nem o que eles estão fazendo”, disse Li na Cúpula da Ásia do Milken Institute, em Cingapura.

Li disse que a empresa decidiu não vender carros de passeio nos EUA por enquanto, apesar de já estar presente no país há “muito tempo”, pois a situação é “complicada”.

“Não temos clareza, visibilidade e estabilidade lá, então decidimos esperar e não entrar no mercado norte-americano de carros de passeio neste momento.”

Li disse que a BYD não tem planos de fazer parcerias com outras empresas chinesas, dada sua liderança em diversas áreas, como armazenamento de energia e painéis solares. “Somos líderes em vários setores, não apenas em automóveis”, afirmou ela.

Li também disse que tem sido difícil contratar pessoal suficiente na China e que a empresa espera utilizar robôs industriais no futuro.

Ela destacou que as ações da BYD na bolsa de Hong Kong estavam “extremamente subvalorizadas” em comparação com as empresas americanas, já que a BYD é uma empresa de engenharia e não apenas uma montadora.

Ela também disse que a Nvidia continua sendo um parceiro “muito forte” na área de chips para a BYD .

articles.title: Corpo de professor é encontrado após 12 dias desaparecido em MT | G1
articles.standfirst: Breno Antônio Humberto de Morais, de 25 anos, estava desaparecido desde a noite de sábado (26), após ser visto saindo de casa, em uma moto.
articles.summary: Breno Antônio Humberto de Morais, de 25 anos, estava desaparecido desde a noite de sábado (25), após ser visto saindo de casa, em uma moto.
articles.body:
Breno Antonio Humberto de Morais está desaparecido desde a noite de sábado (26). — Foto: Reprodução

O corpo do professor Breno Antônio Humberto de Morais, de 25 anos, foi encontrado nesta quinta-feira (8), em um córrego na Rua Juína, no bairro Capão do Pequi, em Várzea Grande , região metropolitana de Cuiabá, após 12 dias de desaparecimento.

A localização ocorreu depois da prisão de Elias Samuel Delgado da Silva, de 26 anos, pai de uma das crianças que estudava na creche onde Breno lecionava. Segundo informações preliminares repassadas à polícia, Elias mora na esquina do local onde o corpo foi encontrado. Ele teria confessado o crime e levado os policiais até o local.

Segundo a defesa de Elias, representada pelo advogado Ronaldo Meirelles, Elias já havia comparecido à delegacia na última sexta-feira (2) para prestar esclarecimentos. Segundo ele, a prisão foi uma surpresa.

"Ele alega que é inocente, só conhecia o professor porque o filho do Elias estuda onde o Breno dá aula", explicou.

Até a última atualização desta reportagem, o advogado ainda não havia conversado com Elias.

O desaparecimento de Breno chamou a atenção da família depois que o irmão gêmeo dele, Bruno Humberto, recebeu mensagens enviadas pelo celular do professor. Segundo Bruno, a forma como os textos foram escritos levantou suspeitas. A família então pediu uma foto para confirmar que Breno estava bem, mas a imagem também causou desconfiança porque as tatuagens que ele tem no braço não apareciam.

Uma câmera de segurança próxima à casa do professor registrou o momento em que ele pegou carona em uma moto na noite de sábado (26) , data em que foi visto pela última vez pelos familiares. Nas imagens, Breno aparece de camiseta preta e short claro, parado próximo a um muro enquanto espera pela moto. Segundo a família, não foi possível identificar o veículo (assista abaixo) .

Outro detalhe que chamou a atenção da família foi a camiseta que Breno usava na foto. Segundo os familiares, a roupa era diferente da que ele vestia quando saiu de casa.

Conforme o irmão, Breno não sai de casa sem avisar ou manter contato com a família. Segundo ele, a pessoa que se passou pelo irmão manteve contato até por volta de 23h30, e 00h desligou o rastreador do aparelho.

articles.title:
Cratera de 4 metros de profundidade se abre na Asa Norte, no DF 
 | G1
articles.standfirst: Buraco se abriu na 714 Norte, próximo à W3, no início da tarde desta quinta-feira (8). Área foi isolada pelo Corpo de Bombeiros; ninguém ficou ferido.
articles.summary: Buraco se abriu na 714 Norte, próximo à W3, no início da tarde desta quinta-feira (8). Área foi isolada pelo Corpo de Bombeiros; ninguém ficou ferido.
articles.body:
O asfalto cedeu e uma cratera se abriu na 714 Norte, próximo à W3 Norte, em Brasília , no início da tarde desta quinta-feira (8). Segundo o Corpo de Bombeiros, ninguém ficou ferido.

De acordo com o Corpo de Bombeiros, o buraco tem cerca de 1,5 metro de diâmetro e 4 metros de profundidade. Ainda não se sabe o que provocou a abertura da cratera.

Pessoas que estavam em um restaurante em frente ao local contaram que ouviram um barulho muito forte e, em seguida, perceberam que o asfalto havia cedido. Segundo os relatos, um carro havia acabado de passar pelo trecho.

Antes da chegada dos bombeiros, pessoas que estavam na região colocaram cadeiras ao redor do buraco para impedir a aproximação. Cerca de 10 minutos depois, os militares chegaram e fizeram o isolamento da área.

Nenhum veículo foi atingido. A Defesa Civil também foi acionada e esteve no local.

articles.title: Projeto em parceria com Ministério da Justiça prevê atender 1,2 mil pessoas em situação de vulnerabilidade no Centro de SP | G1
articles.standfirst: Cais, desenvolvido pelo Casarão Brasil, terá duração inicial de 12 meses e também prevê 2,7 mil participações em atividades coletivas, como cursos e palestras.
articles.summary: Cais, desenvolvido pelo Casarão Brasil, terá duração inicial de 12 meses e também prevê 2,7 mil participações em atividades coletivas, como cursos e palestras.
articles.body:
CAIS, desenvolvido pelo Casarão Brasil, terá duração inicial de 12 meses — Foto: Divulgação

Um projeto em parceria entre o Casarão Brasil – associação LGBTIA+ – e o Ministério da Justiça e Segurança Pública (MJSP) prevê atender 1,2 mil pessoas em situação de vulnerabilidade na região central de São Paulo ao longo de 12 meses. O projeto Cais (Centro de Acesso a Direitos e Inclusão Social) oferece acolhimento e encaminhamentos para serviços de assistência social e saúde, além de apoio para documentação, alimentação e higiene.

A iniciativa também prevê ações de capacitação profissional e inserção produtiva para pessoas que estão fora do mercado de trabalho. O atendimento inicial é destinado à população em situação de rua, sem distinção de idade, gênero ou orientação sexual.

Ailton Rodrigues de Oliveira, coordenador de Projetos do Casarão Brasil, afirma que a iniciativa foi criada diante de situações de vulnerabilidade enfrentadas por pessoas que vivem nas ruas.

"A criação do Cais, que é um projeto criado pelo governo federal, pelo Ministério da Segurança Pública e Secretaria Nacional de Política de Drogas e Gestão de Ativos, está sendo implantado em São Paulo em parceria com o Casarão Brasil, por conta do aumento da criminalidade e marginalização das pessoas que vivem em situação de rua", declarou ao g1 .

"Isso acontece porque essas pessoas vivem situações como dependências química e alcoólica, abandono familiar e carência financeira. Nosso objetivo principal é que essas pessoas tenham acesso aos seus direitos, possam regularizar sua documentação, tenham acesso aos serviços básicos de saúde e a todos os serviços sociais disponíveis pelo governo, para assim retomar à sociedade, como um todo, como qualquer outro indivíduo", completou.

Projeto em parceria entre o Casarão Brasil – Associação LGBTI e o Ministério da Justiça e Segurança Pública (MJSP) prevê atender 1,2 mil pessoas em situação de vulnerabilidade — Foto: Divulgação

A equipe do Cais vai até as ruas para fazer a abordagem inicial. O trabalho envolve agente comunitário, apoio, triagem e serviço social. A partir desse primeiro contato, são identificadas as necessidades de cada pessoa atendida.

"Nós vamos até as ruas com toda a equipe, com agente comunitário, apoio e triagem e serviço social, e lá fazemos abordagem, apresentamos o projeto e aí identificamos quem precisa. Abrimos um PAD, que é o plano de atendimento do acolhido, e listamos quais são as necessidades de urgência ou emergência: quem não tem moradia, ou passa o dia na rua, mas tem casa, tem família, ou é abandono familiar completo, ou não, ou está na dependência química total, como ou só as dificuldades financeiras para a sobrevivência básica", explicou Ailton.

O PAD é utilizado para definir os encaminhamentos necessários, incluindo assistência social, abrigos e unidades de saúde. Antes dos encaminhamentos, é feita uma triagem para verificar as condições físicas da pessoa atendida.

"O PAD é onde acontecem os direcionamentos para assistência social e abrigos e até unidades de saúde, porque precisamos fazer primeiro a triagem de saúde para saber como está o estado físico do acolhido, se precisa de algum tratamento de pressão, diabetes, ISTs, qualquer coisa, até antidepressão, para poder fazer a redução de danos", disse.

Segundo o coordenador, o projeto também conta com parceiros que oferecem locais para acolhimento temporário.

"Depois, a assistência social já vai agir em conjunto, sempre acompanhando. Temos parceiros que oferecem abrigos para pernoite, hotel social, para que os acolhidos possam ter onde dormir, passar uma noite ou então viver temporariamente até se enquadrar novamente na sociedade."

De acordo com Ailton, o acesso à saúde básica está entre as principais necessidades identificadas pela equipe. Ele cita problemas relacionados à alimentação, hidratação e higiene entre as situações que podem agravar as condições de saúde das pessoas em situação de rua.

"A principal demanda é acesso à saúde básica, porque as pessoas já estão em situação ruim; as questões de falta de alimentação e de hidratação levam à desnutrição, a causas de outros tipos de doenças; o contato com outros indivíduos em situação de rua, a falta de higienização, acaba tendo uma contaminação. Então, isso acaba tendo diversos tipos de doenças e casos que a gente precisa imediatamente encaminhá-las para o acesso da saúde."

O segundo caso prioritário entre as demandas, segundo o coordenador, é o suporte jurídico. "Na maioria dos casos, as pessoas não têm documentação. Com isso, precisamos ir a fundo junto com a assistência social, o setor jurídico, buscar a história da pessoa, o cartório, para poder regularizar toda a documentação."

A documentação também é necessária para que as pessoas possam acessar outros serviços.

"Essas são as maiores demandas que nós temos, até para que elas consigam ter os seus próprios benefícios, porque para acessar o serviço de saúde ou qualquer tipo de serviço social, precisa de uma documentação. A gente não deixa o acolhido desamparado."

Projeto prevê cursos e inserção produtiva

Além dos atendimentos individuais, o CAIS prevê pelo menos 2,7 mil participações em atividades coletivas, como rodas de conversa, palestras, encontros, workshops, treinamentos e ações de promoção de hábitos saudáveis e combate ao sedentarismo.

O planejamento também inclui 300 participantes em ações de inserção produtiva e mais de 150 intervenções nessa área.

Ailton afirma que o projeto pretende trabalhar tanto com pessoas que já possuem formação quanto com aquelas que precisam aprender uma nova profissão.

"Como o CAIS não tem discriminação de gênero, idade, escolaridade, de nada, então, nos deparamos com o público que tem escolaridade e que não tem. A nossa contribuição para essa inserção produtiva é qualificar e potencializar o conhecimento das pessoas."

"As pessoas que estão em situação de rua esquecem tudo que já aprenderam na vida, praticamente. Então, é ensinar uma nova profissão, atualizar a profissão da pessoa e que ela se sinta capaz novamente de montar um currículo, entregar um currículo e voltar ao trabalho e que tenha sua renda."

O projeto prevê ainda a participação de empresas e profissionais em oficinas e cursos.

"Nós contamos muito com o apoio de empresas e profissionais que queiram fazer oficinas, cursos, toda a interação aqui para essa inserção produtiva. É dessa forma que o Cais pretende contribuir."

articles.title: Volkswagen Tera ganha novo motor de 128 cv em duas versões, que partem de R$ 134.790 | G1
articles.standfirst: Marca ignora concorrentes de marcas chinesas e aumenta preço de versões Comfort e Highline. SUV compacto recebeu câmbio automático de 8 marchas, mas manteve intacta a lista de equipamentos.
articles.summary: Marca ignora concorrentes de marcas chinesas e aumenta preço de versões Comfort e Highline. SUV compacto recebeu câmbio automático de 8 marchas, mas manteve intacta a lista de equipamentos.
articles.body:
Volkswagen Tera 200 TSI — Foto: divulgação/Volkswagen

A Volkswagen passa a oferecer o Tera com o motor 200 TSI nas versões automáticas Comfort e Highline. O SUV compacto passa a ter motor 1.0 turbo de três cilindros com 128 cv de potência e 20,4 kgfm de torque , associado a um novo câmbio automático de oito marchas .

Antes essas configurações tinham 116 cv de potência e câmbio automático de seis marchas.

A versão Comfort agora custa R$ 134.790 e a Highline sai por R$ 147.190 . Um aumento de preço de R$ 1.600 e R$ 1.000, respectivamente.

O consumo de combustível do Tera 200 em relação ao 170 melhorou na cidade e ficou um pouco abaixo na estrada. Com etanol, são 8,7 km/l na cidade e 10,1 km/l na estrada. Com gasolina, as novas versões do SUV fazem 12,2 km/l na cidade e 14,4 km/l na rodovia.

O restante da linha do Tera continuará usando a calibração de motor 1.0 turbo com 116 cv. Elas também permanecem oferecendo somente câmbio manual.

A concorrência nesse segmento é forte . A CAOA Chery, por exemplo, oferece o modelo Tiggo 5 em duas versões, de R$ 125 mil e R$ 140 mil. O SUV tem motor 1.5 turbo de 143 cv, câmbio CVT, boa lista de equipamentos e maior porte que o Volkswagen.

Além disso, a CAOA Chery oferece o Tiggo 7 Sport com o mesmo motor 1.5 turbo por R$ 141 mil. Isso sem falar no CAOA Changan CS55 Prime por R$ 145 mil.

Na apresentação do Tera, a Volkswagen considerou como concorrentes o Fiat Pulse, o Chevrolet Sonic, o Jeep Avenger e o Renault Kardian. Isso leva em consideração tamanho e conjunto de motor e câmbio, e ignora o preço dos concorrentes chineses de segmento superior.

O g1 já mostrou que os modelos seminovos nessa faixa sofreram uma forte queda de preços . Lançamentos chineses e promoções das marcas tradicionais para encarar as novidades fizeram os usados encalharem.

A principal mudança está justamente no conjunto mecânico. O 200 TSI já é utilizado em outros modelos da Volkswagen, como o T-Cross, e agora chega ao Tera.

De acordo com a marca, o motor entrega torque em baixas rotações, característica que favorece as respostas em situações como saídas, retomadas e ultrapassagens.

A outra novidade é a transmissão automática de oito velocidades. As relações foram distribuídas para manter o motor em uma faixa adequada de funcionamento em diferentes situações.

A proposta é proporcionar trocas mais suaves, acelerações progressivas e rotações mais baixas durante velocidades de cruzeiro.

Na prática, o novo conjunto foi desenvolvido para atuar tanto no trânsito urbano quanto em viagens. O motor de 128 cv e 20,4 kgfm trabalha em conjunto com o câmbio de oito marchas para melhorar as respostas nas retomadas e o conforto durante a condução.

A Volkswagen mantém no Tera os recursos de tecnologia e conectividade já oferecidos pelo SUV. Entre eles estão painel digital, central multimídia VW Play Connect e serviços conectados que podem ser acessados pelo aplicativo Meu VW.

O desenho também não muda com a chegada do novo conjunto.

O Tera mantém ainda a classificação de cinco estrelas no Latin NCAP. Entre os equipamentos citados estão seis airbags, controle eletrônico de estabilidade e sistemas de assistência à condução.

O SUV foi lançado no Brasil em 2025 e, em poucos meses, alcançou a liderança entre os SUVs de entrada e, em 2026, tornou-se o segundo SUV mais vendido do país, atrás apenas do T-Cross.

A produção também ganhou escala. A fábrica de Taubaté (SP) atingiu 100 mil unidades produzidas em menos de um ano.

No mercado internacional, o Tera se tornou em 2026 o modelo mais exportado pela Volkswagen do Brasil. Foram 21.404 unidades embarcadas entre janeiro e julho para 17 mercados da América Latina.

articles.title: Datafolha: como está a disputa de 2º turno para o governo do DF | G1
articles.standfirst: Pesquisa divulgada nesta quinta-feira (8) é a primeira contratada pela Globo e pelo jornal Folha de S.Paulo no 2º turno. A margem de erro é de 3 pontos percentuais.
articles.summary: Pesquisa divulgada nesta quinta-feira (8) é a primeira contratada pela Globo e pelo jornal Folha de S.Paulo no 2º turno. A margem de erro é de 3 pontos percentuais.
articles.body:
Pesquisa Datafolha divulgada nesta quinta-feira (8) mostra como está a disputa para o governo do Distrito Federal para o segundo turno nas eleições de outubro.

A votação será no dia 25 de outubro. Na data, eleitores em todo o país e no exterior também decidirão o segundo turno da eleição presidencial, entre Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) e Lula (PT) .

Celina Leão (PP) e Leandro Grass (PT) — Foto: TV Globo

Veja abaixo os números da pesquisa estimulada, em que o Datafolha mostra aos eleitores entrevistados os nomes dos candidatos:

Datafolha, 8 de outubro: intenção de votos para governador do DF, 2º turno — Foto: Arte/g1

Para 90% dos eleitores ouvidos no levantamento, a escolha do candidato é definitiva. Outros 9% dizem que ainda podem mudar o voto até o segundo turno; 1% não soube dizer.

A pesquisa foi contratada pela Globo e pelo jornal "Folha de S.Paulo". O Datafolha ouviu 910 pessoas entre os dias 6 e 8 de outubro. A margem de erro é de três pontos percentuais, para mais ou para menos. O nível de confiança é de 95%. O número de registro da pesquisa é DF-03365/2026.

A pesquisa divulgada nesta quinta (8) também mediu a avaliação e a aprovação do governo Celina Leão (PP).

➡️ A atual governadora assumiu o cargo em março deste ano – até então, era vice de Ibaneis Rocha (MDB). Ibaneis deixou o governo do DF para disputar o Senado, mas desistiu em seguida .

Segundo a pesquisa Datafolha, 32% dos eleitores consideram a gestão Celina Leão "ótima ou boa" e 29% consideram "ruim ou péssima".

Ótima ou boa: 32% (eram 32% no levantamento anterior, em 1º de outubro );

articles.title: 'Rare' item from Trump's penthouse sells at auction in the Cotswolds
articles.summary: The glass fragment was commissioned by the now-president of the United States almost 40 years ago.
articles.body:
A 24-carat gold section of glass ceiling that once hung above Donald Trump in his New York City penthouse has sold at auction.

The fragment of the bevelled mirror ceiling, described as "unusual and rare" by Dominic Winter Auctioneers, based in the Cotswolds, was commissioned by the now US president for his property at Trump Tower in 1987.

Featuring a leaf pattern, it is believed to be one of only three pieces left from the original commission, which comprised of more than 800ft (243m) of 6in (15cm) wide mirror coffers.

Estimated to fetch between £300-500, the fragment was bought by a private collector in Germany for £380 at the auction house in South Cerney, Gloucestershire, on Wednesday.

A specialist glass studio in California produced the mirrored ceiling that the fragment - measuring 77 x 15cm (30 x 6in) - came from.

The 15cm-wide mirror coffers were produced by the studio for the original project, with more than 12,000 individually cut leaves incorporated into the ceiling over an eight-month period.

A team of specialist polishers worked on the pieces before the gilding was applied.

Trump's penthouse apartment had originally been designed in a more contemporary style, the auctioneers said, but its interiors were "subsequently radically redesigned" in the late 1980s to reflect the president's take on European royal grandeur.

Chris Albury, director at Dominic Winter Auctioneers, previously described the mirror fragment as "an extraordinary survivor from a hugely ambitious decorative project".

He said the "fact that this particular piece was retained as a memento by one of the British craftsmen who worked on the project gives it an especially fascinating provenance".

articles.title: Dad Pays for His Son to Have $150K Leg-Lengthening Surgery to Gain 3 Inches in Height (Exclusive)
articles.summary: Aaron Trinh says he feels “much more at peace” since having the surgery
articles.body:
Ultramarathon runner Aaron Trinh says height discrimination shaped his decision to undergo a leg-lengthening procedure

His father, who is 5'2", supported the surgery after experiencing lifelong insecurity about his own height, and paid the $150,000 cost

Trinh says recovery involved severe nerve pain but believes the surgery was worth it

A man who underwent a painful, pricy leg-lengthening procedure said he doesn't "feel that sense of inadequacy" now that he's three inches taller.

"Seeing how many people around me were much taller than I was, I realized I'm kind of different," ultramarathon runner Aaron Trinh , who was 5'6", tells PEOPLE exclusively about the leg-lengthening procedure he underwent with his father's support in May 2025.

It was his father who paid for the surgery, which is estimated at $150,000. "My dad was easily the first and probably the only person I would come to regarding the surgery, because I know that he would relate to me the most," Trinh tells PEOPLE. "He was the only one who was capable of supporting me throughout this process. He has suffered through height discrimination all his life, starting with his own family to people that were supposed to be his friends, even at the workplace."

His height was something Trinh's father monitored as he grew up, and as he shares, "He'd done a lot of things to proactively make sure I was tall," like "make me drink a glass of milk in the mornings."

His father, who asked to remain anonymous, says that at 5'2", he had long felt "rejected" and "dejected."

"Because of my height. I just feel bad. I feel humiliated," he says, sharing that he avoided socializing because it made him self-conscious. "Can you imagine when you speak to people, you have to look up to them?" he asks. "And when they talk to you, they have to look down and you feel like you're being talked down to all the time."

It was after Trinh was scrolling on TikTok that he saw a video about leg-lengthening surgery. A Google search led him to the Paley Orthopedic & Spine Institute in West Palm Beach.

"My dad offered full financial support for the surgery. It was a really deep father and son connection moment," Trinh says about his father, who says if the technology had been around when he was younger, he also would have undergone the procedure.

They kept it a secret from Trinh's mother until the day before the surgery, where Trinh had his bones broken so metal inserts could be inserted. Using magnets applied externally, the metal stretches the bone to add height, one millimeter a day, over up to four months, as muscles and nerves and other tissue have to gradually grow. After that comes recovery, and learning to walk again.

Take PEOPLE with you! Subscribe to PEOPLE magazine to get the latest details on celebrity news, exclusive royal updates, how-it-happened true crime stories and more — right to your mailbox.

Trinh says he was "extremely nervous" on the day of the surgery — which he called the "easiest part" of the whole process. The "lowest" part, he tells PEOPLE, was the nerve pain, which left him crying out in pain at times. Still, he called it "manageable."

About eight months after the surgery, Trinh says he became aware of his new height. "Things were shrinking," he says. He would have to reach out his arm to grab something that had previously been closer. That's when he realized, "This is actually becoming a reality."

Trinh's first surgery was a year ago; he needed a second surgery to remove the hardware from his leg. Now 5'9", he's focused on moving forward.

"Now that my height dysphoria is gone, I can mentally focus on a lot of other things" like graduation, his career, and a social life — what he calls "things that any normal human being would love to just focus on."

"I am absolutely much more at peace with my mind and my body, and I think that's gonna stick around for a very long time," he says. "This surgery was purely just for my self-fulfillment, just so that I could be able to mentally focus on other things."

The surgery, he says, was a "necessity" — and not a punchline. "I don't think anyone has the right to judge," Trinh says. "It's no different from wanting to work hard to improve yourself just as much as if you were wanting to go to the gym."

articles.title: ‘Extraordinary measure rendered ordinary’: Madhya Pradesh High Court slams ‘reckless’ NSA use
articles.summary: Madhya Pradesh High Court quashes NSA detention of two brothers, slams reckless use, cites SC ruling, stresses Articles 14, 19, 21 safeguards.
articles.body: BHOPAL: Madhya Pradesh High Court has criticised the “reckless invocation” of the National Security Act (NSA), while quashing the preventive detention of two brothers under the law and warning that an extraordinary constitutional measure was being treated as an ordinary course of proceedings.A division bench headed by Justice Vivek Agarwal ordered the release of Rajendra Thakur and Rajesh Thakur, ruling that authorities failed to establish the requisite grounds for preventive detention and appeared to have acted without applying their minds. The Jabalpur district collector had ordered their detention on Jan 6 for three months over an alleged threat to public order, later extending the period.“Preventive detention, conceived as an extraordinary measure by the framers of our Constitution, has been rendered ordinary with its reckless invocation over the years as if it were available for use even in the ordinary course of proceedings,” HC said.The order, delivered on Sept 11, was made public on Oct 5.The court found that the brothers, named in 14 cases, had been acquitted in 11 when NSA was invoked against them. “This leads to a conclusion that correct facts were not placed before the competent authority, and that clearly suffers from the vice of non-application of mind,” the bench said.It added that authorities could have verified their criminal records with minimal effort through the Crime and Criminal Tracking Network and Systems. The three pending cases against the duo pertained to obscene act, causing hurt and wrongful confinement, and throwing a crude bomb to create unrest.The bench was also alarmed that the proposal by the city SP to invoke NSA and the collector’s detention order passed through four officials and were completed on the same day.“Turning our attention to section 3(1) of the NSA, the govt has to arrive at a subjective satisfaction that a goonda (as in the present case) has to be detained, in order to prevent him from acting in a manner prejudicial to the maintenance of public order. The application of mind to invoke the aforesaid extraordinary measure appears to be missing in the present case,” the HC said.“There is no requisite satisfaction recorded by the detaining authority that the detenus are a threat to public order. It also appears that the haste with which the matter was processed in a single day took away independent exercise of mind by the detaining authority,” it added.Citing the Supreme Court’s 2023 ruling in Ameena Begum vs State of Telangana, the bench stressed that constitutional safeguards must be enforced to prevent arbitrary detention.“To unchain the shackles of preventive detention, it is important that safeguards enshrined in our Constitution, particularly under the ‘golden triangle’ formed by Articles 14, 19 and 21, are diligently enforced,” the court said.The ruling comes amid similar judicial criticism of NSA detentions in Uttar Pradesh. Last month, Allahabad HC ordered the release of Delhi University graduate Aakriti Choudhary, detained in connection with a workers’ protest in April, and imposed a fine of Rs 5 lakh on Noida DM and other officials.In its Sept 2 order, Allahabad HC rebuked UP’s administrative machinery for invoking NSA without applying its mind or relying on credible evidence. It stressed that preventive detention was an exception, not a substitute for ordinary criminal law.Reminding police and administrative officials that their allegiance was to the Constitution, not the political executive, Allahabad HC warned that an errant bureaucracy could reduce UP to an Orwellian dystopia.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Bhopal | Silver Rate in Bhopal | Bank Holidays in Bhopal | Public Holidays in Bhopal | Petrol Price in Bhopal | Diesel Price in Bhopal | CNG Price in Bhopal | LPG Price in BhopalStay updated with the latest Bhopal news. articles.title: Richard Branson was 29 when he bought an island to impress a girl, offered $100,000 for a $6 million property; in 2007, he bought 125-acre Moskito Island for $15 million, now divided among nine families
articles.summary: Long before Sir Richard Branson became a billionaire entrepreneur with a global business empire, he was a young businessman looking for a way to impress
articles.body: Long before Sir Richard Branson became a billionaire entrepreneur with a global business empire, he was a young businessman looking for a way to impress the woman he had fallen in love with.His idea was extraordinary, buy an island.In 1978, Branson learned that a 74-acre island in the British Virgin Islands was on the market. The property was Necker Island, and its name immediately caught his attention because of its connection to the Virgin brand he had launched in 1970 as a mail-order record business. Virgin’s own timeline confirms that Branson purchased Necker Island in 1978.The entrepreneur later recalled the unusual circumstances surrounding the purchase in an essay published on Virgin’s website.Branson wrote that when he heard an island sharing a name with his company was for sale, his immediate reaction was to contact the people selling it.At the time, however, he admitted that he was still in the early stages of building Virgin Records and did not have the money required to purchase a private island.There was, however, another reason he was willing to try.Branson had fallen for Joan Templeman.Branson wanted to impress Joan TemplemanIn his account, Branson recalled that he had been trying to find a way to impress the woman he had fallen for, which prompted him to contact the island’s realtor.The response was more encouraging than he could have expected.The realtor offered Branson an all-expenses-paid trip to the British Virgin Islands to see the property. Branson agreed, but only on the condition that he could bring a guest.That guest was Templeman, who would later become his wife. Branson has since described Joan as the inspiration behind his decision to buy Necker Island. In a 2023 post on Virgin’s website, he wrote that he originally bought the island “in an effort to impress her.”The trip succeeded romantically, but the island itself appeared to be well beyond Branson’s financial reach.The island was priced at $6 million, but Branson offered $100,000The realtor quoted Branson a discounted asking price of $6 million for Necker Island.For a young entrepreneur still establishing Virgin Records, that figure was impossible.Branson nevertheless made an offer.He offered $100,000, the highest amount he could afford at the time.The realtor was reportedly unimpressed. Branson later recalled that he and Templeman were left to find their own way home after the offer failed to impress.But the rejection did not end Branson’s interest in the island.A year later, he discovered that Necker Island had still not been sold.This time, Branson returned with a larger offer of $180,000.The seller accepted.There was one condition attached to the deal, Branson had to build a resort on the island within four years.What had begun as an ambitious attempt to impress a woman had suddenly become a major property acquisition for a young entrepreneur whose fortune was still in its early stages.Necker Island became Branson’s private Caribbean retreatNecker Island is now one of the most recognisable properties associated with Branson.Virgin Limited Edition describes it as a 74-acre private island in the British Virgin Islands, surrounded by coral reefs and white-sand beaches. The property can be hired exclusively, while selected dates also allow individual guests to book rooms without taking over the entire island.The island has also remained closely connected to the Branson family. Virgin’s own account describes the memories Branson and Templeman created there over the years, with Branson calling the decision to buy it one of the best he ever made.But Necker Island was not the end of Branson’s private-island ambitions.In 2007, Branson bought the larger Moskito IslandNearly three decades after acquiring Necker, Branson expanded his Caribbean property portfolio.In 2007, he purchased the 125-acre Moskito Island, located roughly two miles from Necker Island in the British Virgin Islands. PEOPLE reports that Branson paid $15 million for the property.Unlike Necker Island, however, Moskito Island eventually evolved into a private residential community with multiple owners.According to PEOPLE, Branson began developing the island in the mid-2010s and divided it into 10 residential lots that were made available to private buyers. Today, nine private families are reported to own estates on the island, including Branson himself.Several wealthy families now own estates on Moskito IslandAmong the reported owners are Real Housewives of New York cast member Erika Hammond and her husband, Ankur Jain.Their ownership of a property on Moskito Island became a talking point on the reality show, with Hammond discussing the island’s private nature and its multiple family owners.Other reported owners include Paul Salem, chairman of MGM Resorts, as well as technology entrepreneurs Michael and Xochi Birch.Although individual estates are privately owned, residents share access to common amenities and jointly maintain parts of the island, including beaches and tennis courts.The result is an unusual arrangement, a private island community where several wealthy families own individual estates while sharing parts of the surrounding infrastructure.Moskito Island is also open to luxury holidaymakersBranson’s private-island portfolio is not entirely closed to outside visitors.In 2021, he announced that properties on Moskito Island could be rented by guests. PEOPLE reports that three villas are available for year-round rentals, offering visitors the opportunity to stay on an island otherwise divided among private owners.Virgin Limited Edition also lists both Necker Island and Moskito Island among its collection of luxury retreats.A $180,000 gamble became a private-island legacyBranson’s island story began when he was still a young entrepreneur who could not afford the $6 million asking price for Necker Island.He first offered $100,000, failed, returned a year later and eventually secured the 74-acre property for $180,000.The motivation was deeply personal, he wanted to impress Joan Templeman, the woman who would become his wife.Decades later, that youthful gamble sits at the heart of one of the most unusual chapters of Branson’s business and personal life. Necker became a luxury private retreat, while his later purchase of Moskito Island evolved into a private residential community shared by a group of wealthy families.You use AI every day. articles.title: South Africa protests turn violent amid rage over asylum ruling
articles.summary: Several cars torched and foreign-run businesses forced to shut in Johannesburg’s Soweto and coastal city of Durban.
articles.body:
Anti-migrant protests in two cities in South Africa have turned ⁠violent, with the government blaming disinformation about a court ruling on asylum seekers.

Violence erupted on Thursday in Johannesburg’s Soweto township and the east coast port city of Durban, with two dozens cars set ablaze and foreign-run businesses forced to close, police said.

The unrest followed demonstrations demanding that refugee centres stop processing asylum applications.

Acting National Police Commissioner Lieutenant General Puleng Dimpane on Thursday said 10 vehicles were torched in Johannesburg and 14 in Durban, where three people were arrested.

In Soweto, a Reuters reporter saw residents carrying groceries out of a shop they said was owned by a person from Somalia, whom they chased away. Those residents fled after police arrived.

In Durban, a Reuters reporter saw cars torched in the urban centre, where foreign-owned shops were also looted. AFP reporters in the city said police opened fire with rubber bullets to disperse protesters who reportedly set alight a business run by foreigners.

The protesters are opposed to a July Constitutional Court decision that removes procedural barriers to seeking asylum, including for people who entered South Africa irregularly, lacked asylum transit visas, or missed reporting deadlines.

On Thursday, the government’s Inter-Ministerial Committee on Migration held an urgent briefing to address overcrowding at asylum offices after implementing the ruling. A day prior, the committee said all its offices were overwhelmed by the number of incoming applications.

Government spokesperson William Baloyi said ‌the violence was triggered by people spreading deliberately false information about the constitutional court ruling.

Baloyi said the court decision had been widely misrepresented, and that it did not automatically grant refugee status, permanent residence or other legal rights to undocumented migrants.

“We are ⁠deeply concerned by what is going on now,” he added.

Months of protests by populist, anti-immigrant groups against undocumented foreign nationals, demanding they leave South Africa, have led tens of thousands to flee, some repatriated by their governments.

Three decades since apartheid ended, South Africa remains deeply unequal and about a third of people are out of work. Migrants are often blamed for taking jobs, fuelling crime and straining public services, although such claims are not supported by evidence.

articles.title: Cardiff University 'banter' account criticised for sexual assault posts
articles.summary: Cardiff University has since unfollowed the account after concerns were raised about the "harmful" material.
articles.body:
Warning: This article contains references to sexual assault that readers may find distressing.

A university has been criticised after anonymous accounts of sexual assault and misogynistic posts were made on social media by a student-run "banter" account it followed.

Cardiff University has since unfollowed the Cardiff Uni Banter Instagram account after students raised concerns about the material being posted.

One post included an anonymous confession describing a man continuing to have sex with a woman while she was having a seizure.

Cardiff University said sexual violence and harassment and all forms of gender-based violence would "not be tolerated", adding that fact that it had followed the account was not "in any way an endorsement". Cardiff Uni Banter was asked to comment.

It is not known if the claim made in the post is true, but some of the page's content has received hundreds of likes and has been widely reshared.

Jennifer Taylor, National Union of Students Cymru president, said the comments were "dangerous, harmful and are reinforcing a toxic culture on our campuses that must be tackled head on".

The Instagram account describes itself as a place for "the best confessions, memes and banter in Cardiff" and has more than 14,000 followers. It publishes anonymous submissions from students covering university life, relationships, sex, and nightlife.

Megan Elmer contacted the BBC after becoming concerned about the content, saying she believes it "contributes to the perpetuation of rape culture by normalising misogynistic attitudes and discussions of sexual violence".

Megan said she did not know whether the anonymous allegations published by the account were true, but believed the posts raised questions about the culture surrounding sexual violence within the university community.

She said she was particularly concerned that Cardiff University's official Instagram account had been following Cardiff Uni Banter.

"I would therefore be interested in whether the university is aware of the account and its content, whether it has received any reports or concerns relating to the account, and why its official Instagram account follows the page," she said.

"Imagine being a woman who has been raped or sexually assaulted at university, maybe even one of those girls whose sexual violence has made the account.

"How would you feel if your own university followed that account."

Some students are calling for a boycott of the social media page, with other posts seen by BBC Wales describing women as "sluzzers", and "tarts".

Rebecca Rumsey, 23, a Cardiff University student and co-founder of the sexual misconduct campaign group Time To Act, said students had repeatedly sent the group screenshots of the posts.

"We got sent the posts hundreds of times by students," she said. "We tried to reach out to the page — they still haven't responded."

Time To Act called for students to unfollow the account, stop submitting confessions and report content they believed promoted sexual violence or misogyny.

Rebecca said the backlash had resulted in the account losing about 2,000 followers.

"There's a lot of misogynistic and rape culture posts on that page, and it's not good enough," she said. "It's not banter."

Cardiff University said it was aware of the account and the "concerning nature of the posts" but emphasised the account was "not affiliated or associated with Cardiff University, nor are we aware who is responsible for it".

A university spokesperson said: "This is not just banter. As a university we're committed to creating a safe, respectful, and inclusive environment where everyone has the right to feel safe and treated with dignity and respect."

It added that it had received complaints about the account, had reported posts and the account itself, and would continue to do so.

"We followed the account so we could actively monitor and report such posts. We unfollowed the account in response to the concerns expressed by our Students' Union and from staff, students and members of the public."

Cardiff Uni Banter has been approached for comment.

articles.title: Family of immigrant dad fatally shot by ICE files claim against government, saying death was preventable
articles.summary: Silverio Villegas González was killed in a traffic stop after he had dropped off his two young children in a suburb of Chicago.
articles.body: The family of a Mexican father fatally shot by an ICE officer in a Chicago suburb last year took the first steps in a lawsuit against the federal government over misconduct they say led to his unlawful killing, according to the legal team representing the man’s estate. Silverio Villegas González, 38, died during a traffic stop on the morning of Sept. 12, 2025, just after he had dropped off his 8-year-old son at school and his 4-year-old son at daycare. The ICE officers who pulled Villegas over and eventually killed him were conducting immigration arrests as part of the enforcement surge in Chicago known as “Operation Midway Blitz.” The MacArthur Justice Center filed a complaint under the Federal Tort Claims Act on Thursday on behalf of Villegas’ estate. The complaint, which was obtained by NBC News, cites the medical examiner’s findings that the ICE officer was standing alongside and not in front of Villegas’ car, thus shooting him downward into his neck. According to the claim, this resulted in the officer “effectively executing Silverio at close range” and killing him “unjustifiably, unnecessarily, and contrary to DHS policy.” “There’s been zero accountability. It’s shocking. It’s been more than a year, and we don’t even know the name of an ICE officer who killed a person on our streets. This is not normal,” Jonathan Manes, senior counsel at the MacArthur Justice Center, told NBC News. “So, we’re bringing this claim to demand accountability.” Though federal agents cannot be directly sued, the FTCA claim allows private citizens to sue the federal government and seek damages. The claim is the first formal step before filing a federal lawsuit in the upcoming months against the U.S. over Villegas’ death, Manes said. The Department of Homeland Security did not respond to a request for comment about the claims filed by Villegas’ family on Thursday. At the time of Villegas’ fatal shooting, DHS said Villegas resisted arrest and attempted to flee — injuring the agent, who, “fearing for his own life,” opened fire. The ICE officers involved were not wearing body cameras, and no video evidence that emerged at the time showed the actual shooting or the ICE agent being dragged and injured. Eventually, a combination of surveillance video from nearby businesses and body cameras from local police officers who responded to the shooting showed that two ICE officers approached Villegas’ car and leaned on his window frames. The videos show Villegas reversed about 50 feet and began to drive away into the open traffic lane. As one agent chased the vehicle, gunshots were heard before Villegas’ car was seen crashing into a parked delivery truck. Based on the evidence from the medical examiner’s report and an investigation from the Illinois Accountability Commission, the officer who fatally shot Villegas “was standing alongside the vehicle. He wasn’t in the vehicle’s path, and Silverio was just trying to drive away,” Manes said. “Whatever you think about driving away from a traffic stop, it does not allow an American police officer or immigration officer to shoot and kill a person. That is clear,” Manes said, adding that this is even contrary to DHS’ policy. DHS policy states that deadly force should not be used against someone whose actions are only a threat to themselves or property. This does not apply if the person poses an “imminent threat of death or serious physical injury to the officer” or anyone else, according to a 2023 report from the U.S. Government Accountability Office. The policy also states that “firearms shall not be discharged solely to disable moving vehicles.” Under new internal guidance, ICE officers have been ordered not to engage in high-speed car chases and to make vehicle stops only if they have completed specific agency training courses. Both the family of Renee Good, who was fatally shot in her car by an ICE officer during “Operation Metro Surge” in Minneapolis in January, and Marimar Martinez, who survived being shot five times by a Border Patrol agent in Chicago while driving, have recently sued the federal government seeking damages months after initially filing similar FTCA claims.

articles.title: Epstein survivor Annie Farmer supports drive to remove Leslie Wexner’s name from OSU campus
articles.summary: Former students have accused Ohio State of failing to protect them from a campus doctor who preyed on them while Wexner was on the OSU board of trustees.
articles.body: The former Ohio State University students who sued the school alleging it failed to protect them from being sexually abused by a campus doctor got a shoutout of support Thursday from one of the first women to blow the whistle on Jeffrey Epstein. Annie Farmer, who says both she and her sister Maria were among the hundreds of women victimized by the now-dead financier, said she supports their push to have the name of Leslie Wexner, the Ohio billionaire who once bankrolled Epstein, removed from campus buildings. Farmer also criticized OSU leaders for waging a prolonged legal battle, settled in June, with the hundreds of men who said the university did nothing to stop Dr. Richard Strauss from sexually assaulting them decades ago, often under the guise of doing physicals. The Strauss survivors have noted repeatedly that Wexner served on the OSU Board of Trustees during the time period that the campus doctor preyed on them. “Hundreds of students and alumni have made it clear that they do not want Wexner’s name on their buildings including many of the brave athletes who are survivors of Richard Strauss,” Farmer said in an emailed response to questions from NBC News. “If you are an OSU student who has been a victim of a sexual assault you are currently directed to go to the Wexner Medical Center for an exam. That is highly problematic.” Farmer was in Columbus with the Donald J. Trump and Jeffrey Epstein Memorial Reading Room, a traveling public art installation that includes 3.5 million pages of partially redacted Department of Justice documents related to Epstein. A spokesperson for Wexner declined to comment. Meanwhile, OSU spokesperson Benjamin Johnson did not directly respond to Farmer’s remarks but said the university has an established process for considering renaming requests. “We have received requests related to Les Wexner, and they remain under review,” Johnson said in an email. The billionaire’s name is on the Les Wexner Football Complex, the Wexner Center for the Arts and the Ohio State University Wexner Medical Center. Farmer told investigators that she was 16 years old in 1996 when Epstein and his accomplice Ghislaine Maxwell invited her to Epstein’s New Mexico ranch under the pretense of helping her with her education. But when she got there, Farmer said, they sexually assaulted her. Her testimony helped convict Maxwell in 2021 of sex trafficking and other charges. Maxwell is currently serving a 20-year prison sentence. Epstein, who was charged in 2019 with sex trafficking of minors, died in a New York City jail while awaiting trial, and his death was ruled a suicide. President Donald Trump, who was once a close friend of Epstein’s, has never been accused by authorities of any wrongdoing connected to Epstein. He had also denied any wrongdoing. Farmer said there are parallels between what happened to the hundreds of women Epstein groomed and preyed on and what happened to the young men Strauss targeted when he worked at OSU from 1978 through 1998. Strauss killed himself in 2005. “Both illustrate the tremendous harm that predators can cause when they are surrounded by a network of enablers who look the other way because it is uncomfortable or inconvenient to acknowledge their crimes,” Farmer said. Farmer noted that Strauss’ abuse was exposed only because of the “bravery of whistleblowers like Stephen Snyder-Hill and Michael DiSabato.” DiSabato, a former OSU wrestler, led the charge to hold the university accountable. Snyder-Hill, also a former OSU student and Strauss survivor, emerged as an outspoken critic of his alma mater. “My sister, Maria Farmer, has long been grateful for the way this group of brave men has spoken out,” Farmer said. Back in 2020, a group of former OSU wrestlers formally asked Ohio Inspector General Randall Meyer to investigate allegations that Maria Farmer was assaulted in 1996 by Epstein at an Ohio property “owned and secured” by Wexner. Wexner, who said he cut ties with Epstein in 2007 after the first allegations surfaced that he was trafficking in and sexually abusing young women, has denied knowing Maria Farmer and having any knowledge of her alleged assault. Wexner has denied any wrongdoing related to Epstein. Meyer’s office did not immediately respond to a request to find out if those allegations were ever investigated. A search of news databases uncovered no news articles indicating that his office looked into the allegations. DiSabato also led the drive to remove Wexner’s name from the OSU campus buildings the Victoria’s Secret founder helped fund. He did so while a group of 279 Strauss survivors was locked in a legal battle with the university. The former wrestler was one of 317 plaintiffs who had settled their lawsuits against OSU earlier. In June, OSU agreed to pay $100 million in damages to the 279 former students. Currently, a special master is in the process of determining how to divide the nine-figure settlement with these claimants.

articles.title: Two men arrested after breaking into UK airbase used by US, counterterrorism police say
articles.summary: British counterterrorism police are investigating after two Latvian men were arrested inside a Royal Air Force base used by US personnel, authorities said on Thursday.
articles.body: British counterterrorism police are investigating after two Latvian men were arrested inside a Royal Air Force base used by US personnel, authorities said on Thursday. The arrests come weeks after a suspected plot targeting another British airbase used by the US military raised concerns about security at military sites across Britain. Police said there was nothing so far to suggest the incident at RAF Molesworth in eastern England was linked to the suspected plot against RAF Fairford in western England, which has been used by the US military to launch missions against Iran. The men were discovered after Ministry of Defence Police found an abandoned vehicle during a security patrol at RAF Molesworth, about 100 km (60 miles) north of London, and raised the alarm. Subsequent checks uncovered a small breach in the perimeter fence and the two men, aged 32 and 36, were arrested inside the base. They were initially arrested on suspicion of trespassing on a prohibited site and criminal damage, before being re-arrested on suspicion of “entering a prohibited place for a purpose prejudicial to the UK” under the National Security Act 2023. ‘Highly vigilant’ RAF Molesworth is used by US personnel and hosts intelligence analysis and command operations, as well as a NATO intelligence centre. It is not used for flying operations. Last month, several men were arrested over a suspected plot to attack RAF Fairford, 90 miles (145 km) ‌west of London. The British government has linked the suspected plot to Iran, which denied any involvement. The incident raised concerns over security at Britain’s military bases, particularly those used by US forces. The US said on Monday that a threat linked to Iran had prompted the removal of its bombers from Fairford. “We’re very aware of the recent heightened interest and concern around military sites, but at this stage there is nothing to suggest this incident is connected to the events at RAF Fairford last week,” Helen Flanagan, head of Counter Terrorism Policing London, said in a statement. Police said both men were resident in Britain and that officers were searching two addresses in the area around Peterborough, a nearby city. Bomb disposal officers checked the abandoned vehicle but found nothing of concern, police said. “We are highly vigilant about potential threats to our military sites and work closely with the police to keep them secure,” defense minister Wes Streeting said in a post on X. A US Air Force spokesperson said they appreciated the swift response and support from local law enforcement. “We remain in close coordination with our UK partners to help ensure the safety and security of both our military and local communities,” the spokesperson added.

articles.title: ABC News deletes ‘hit piece’ on Trump sons' Pentagon-linked investments without explanation
articles.summary: ABC News quietly deleted its report on Donald Trump Jr. and Eric Trump's alleged ties to Pentagon contracts after 1789 Capital threatened legal action.
articles.body: ABC News deleted a report criticizing the business dealings of President Donald Trump’s oldest sons, Donald Trump Jr. and Eric Trump, Thursday after facing legal threats but has failed to provide any explanation or editor’s note for the vanished "hit piece." The now-deleted report, which can still be viewed via the Internet Archive’s Wayback Machine, was published Wednesday with the headline, "Trump sons' investments have won billions in Pentagon contracts since his election," and said Anduril, the company investing in a new Baltimore shipyard, had ties to Donald Trump Jr. and Eric Trump. "1789 Capital — a venture capital firm that lists Donald Trump Jr. as one of six partners along with three founders — claimed a major stake in Anduril in June 2025 from a $2.5 billion investment into the company," ABC News reported in the deleted story. TRUMP TURNS TO EMERGING TECH GIANT IN MULTI-BILLION BID TO RAMP UP US SUBMARINE PRODUCTION "Since that investment, Anduril has been awarded 135 other contracts with the U.S. government and to date has received around $1.8 billion from those agreements, according to active defense contracts posted to SAM.gov, the official system for government contracting. "The company is one of the largest manufacturers to receive an investment from Donald Trump Jr. and his brother Eric Trump, but they are not the only one." Alexa Henning, a spokesperson for 1789 Capital and a former chief of staff to the director of national intelligence, took to social media, insisting the company does not have a "major stake" in Anduril and blasting the "biased hit piece." "Here's a small lesson, that I also explained to ABC, the ‘reporter’ who is a complete idiot conflated raising funds with investment by 1789. Those are two separate actions," Henning wrote. "Meaning the ‘investments’ mentioned were actually the total number raised for a funding round, that MANY companies contribute to," Henning continued. "Another thing that the reporter buried the lead on was that many of these companies have gotten government contracts during Biden AND Trump, which completely negates the assertion by ABC that Don Jr and Eric Trump are doing anything wrong." JARED KUSHNER SCOLDS CNN OVER 'DEEPLY MISLEADING’ REPORT, SAYS KEY INFO BURIED BEHIND PAYWALL Shortly after, ABC News deleted the story from its website. The link to the original report now states, "This page either does not exist or is currently unavailable." ABC News did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The network has not issued a correction or provided a public explanation for why the report was removed from its website. ABC News also deleted a viral X post intended to promote the story that was shared by several prominent Democrats. Henning spoke to Fox News Digital after ABC News deleted the story. She said that in addition to calling out the story publicly on X, she sent a detailed email to ABC News pointing out mistakes in the reporting and informing the Disney-owned network that lawyers would be in touch if action was not taken. She said she "really appreciates that they took it down" but wants a clear explanation of why it was published in the first place and believes ABC News should inform readers of its errors. ‘LIBELOUS’ NYT REPORT TYING TRUMP FAMILY TO GOVERNMENT-BACKED DEAL SPARKS LEGAL DEMAND Henning also told Fox News Digital that ABC News never asked 1789 Capital for comment prior to the story’s initial publication despite being mentioned several times in the initial report. "The majority of people reporting on 1789 do not fundamentally understand how it works," she said. Once the story had vanished, Trump Jr. responded to California Gov. Gavin Newsom, who had shared the initial ABC News report on X. "ABC deleted this article in less than 24 hours because it’s false. Sounds about as long as your presidential campaign would last," Trump Jr. wrote. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Fox News Digital’s Morgan Phillips contributed to this report.

articles.title: Head of maternity review says 'We will listen to parents'
articles.summary: The woman leading a national review into maternity services in Scotland promises her work will consider parents' experiences.
articles.body:
The head of a major review of maternity services has reassured bereaved parents their voices will be heard as part of her work.

Families had expressed concern the forward-looking national review of services in Scotland would not take into account how they felt failed by the NHS.

But Prof Christine McCourt told BBC Scotland talking to a range of people would be valuable in "drawing the right lessons for improvement".

The Scottish government said the review, which got under way this week and is due to report back next summer, would consider the "direct experiences of women, families and staff at every level of care".

The review was ordered by ministers a year ago following a BBC Disclosure investigation highlighting failings in maternity care across Scotland.

In the film, Lori Quate shared his experience of losing his wife Jacqui Hunter in 2020.

Jacqui died at Ninewells hospital in Dundee while giving birth to their stillborn daughter, Olivia.

She had been given an overdose of a drug to bring on labour, and an NHS review found that it could have been a factor in her death.

The Scottish government announced an independent national review of maternity care a month after the documentary heard calls from families, NHS staff and experts for urgent action to improve safety.

'My wife died in childbirth but wasn't told she'd been given labour drug overdose'

As the review got under way this week, Lori said it was not clear what would feed into its findings.

"The biggest concern was that the phrase 'forward-looking' seems to necessitate a limited involvement of families who have been through the mill of this culture of failings," he said.

"How are they going to face forwards if they're not willing to hear from the families?"

"I understand you can't go looking at every single individual case if it's about changing the system," he added.

"But a case like Jacqui and Olivia's is almost exemplary of the systemic rot and failings that prevail throughout the entire system."

McCourt, a professor of maternal and child health at City St George's at the University of London, is chairing the review.

She said it was important to hear from parents with both negative and positive views.

"It's not part of our remit to investigate individual cases," she said. "But there's a great potential to learn from people's experience, especially if you actually talk to a range of people.

"You can draw out the patterns in the general lessons. What led to a poor outcome in the first place, and then what happened afterwards?

"Are parents getting honest, useful explanations? Are they getting support?"

The review will also build on themes that have emerged from safety inspections of maternity units, including the need to listen to families, investigate serious incidents fully and learn from mistakes.

McCourt said she wouldn't shy away from identifying pressures in the system such as staffing shortages.

"We're completely independent, so we have that capacity to feel totally free to say what we need to say," she said

"You can't run an effective health service with staff who are excessively anxious, as well as not having the right mix of staff and the right numbers of staff."

While she said she would take into account lessons learned by previous inquiries in England and other parts of the UK, McCourt said Scotland had different challenges.

"You've got a much more dispersed population in Scotland. So thinking about how to cater for the more rural areas where you've got long distances, and you've got a smaller population concentration, that's quite different from most of England.

"So there are going to be things that are quite distinct about Scotland, as well as the fact that you do have devolution in the health system."

Announcing the beginning of the review earlier this week, the Scottish government said it would look at inequalities such as the higher rates of maternal death among Black and Asian women.

The review will also have a "specific focus" on maternity services in Caithness, Elgin and Wigtownshire, where there are longstanding campaigns to improve local services.

Claire Fleming's third child Andrew was born in Dumfries, 70 miles from her home just outside Stranraer, after the local maternity unit closed in 2018 .

She travelled that distance even for short antenatal appointments.

She does not expect the review to lead to the full reinstatement of a 24-hour maternity service in Stranraer.

"I understand there are constraints and problems in recruiting midwives and staff, so I'm not asking for that. But what I do think is really important is that the absolute basics are covered here, and they're not getting done just now," she said.

"So when they find out what is going on down here in Wigtownshire, they need to act on it.

"I have been campaigning for more than five years, and I have met every MP and the first minister. I've spoken to them all and nothing's changing, so I am praying this is the thing that changes something."

Health Secretary Angela Constance said the independent review would sit alongside ongoing inspections of every acute maternity unit in Scotland.

"While the vast majority of mothers receive good care, I have heard from families who were let down," she said.

"Their experiences must shape improvement."

McCourt said she wanted to hear from people in different areas across Scotland.

"We need to take account of the different mix of services and how best to make sure that people have good access, that people feel that they have safe access as well.

"Anybody that wants to talk to us, that's very welcome."

Patients and staff who want to contribute to the review can find the details here .
