articles.title: A CEO who was not a cyclist trained for months, then rode about 2,000 miles from Mexico to Canada in 12 days; along the route, his team raised and distributed more than $766,000 to over 70 people and organisations
articles.summary: Matt King, CEO of Gobundance, had never considered himself a cyclist.
articles.body: Matt King, CEO of Gobundance, had never considered himself a cyclist. But after being inspired by a friend who participated in a charity run across Texas, King decided to take on an ambitious challenge of his own, cycling nearly 2,000 miles from Mexico to Canada while raising money for people in small towns along the route.According to PEOPLE, King ultimately completed the journey in 12 days, one day faster than his original target, while raising more than $766,000 and distributing financial support to more than 70 individuals and organisations.From an old bicycle to a 2,000-mile challengeFor years, King said he wanted to make a meaningful impact but felt he was mostly “just talking about it.” That changed when he watched a friend take part in a charity run across Texas.The experience gave him the idea for theRIDE, a cycling journey from Mexico to Canada covering approximately 2,000 miles. His original plan was to complete it in 13 days and raise $1 million through the challenge.The money would then be distributed directly to people in rural communities who needed financial assistance.There was, however, one significant obstacle. King was not a cyclist.At the time, the 36-year-old's only bicycle was an old one hanging on a wall with two flat tyres. He bought a new bike and gave himself five and a half months to prepare.Training began at 4 a.m.King trained under the guidance of Colorado professional cyclist, endurance coach and sports nutritionist Joey Hassett. His preparation involved spending hours every day cycling on an indoor trainer at his Texas home.He often began training at 4 a.m. so that he could finish before his wife and three young children, aged between one and seven, started their day.The months of preparation were put to the test almost immediately after the ride began on May 27.On the first day, the team encountered torrential rain and winds reaching 30 mph. King compared the experience to being hit by a BB gun. The riders stopped for four hours when the storm became particularly severe before continuing late into the night to make up the lost time.The problems did not stop there. King broke a cycling shoe, had a shoe clip replaced and, before the team had even left Texas, their support van reportedly broke down 13 times.Yet King continued, keeping the purpose of the journey in mind.“I just keep telling myself we chose (to do) this hard (ride) so that we can provide a direct impact to the people who didn't get to choose the hard that they've been handed,” he said.Finding people in need along the routeRather than relying solely on organised applications, King and his team looked for people to help by speaking to residents and businesses in the communities they passed through.They would walk into coffee shops and ask people to share stories of individuals or families who could use financial assistance.The resulting acts of generosity varied widely. The team sometimes left $1,000 tips at restaurants or paid $400 at a car wash run by a girls' volleyball team for a service that normally cost $40.In one case, they gave a mother $20,000 to help her purchase a new car.Mother receives $20,000 for a new carOne of the recipients was Amy Hernandez, 46, a substitute teacher in Dilley, Texas, whose 25-year-old son Seth has autism and epilepsy.Hernandez's car had no rear air vents, so she used two plastic fans attached to the back of the headrest to help keep her son cool. The Texas heat could trigger his seizures, making travel particularly difficult.According to PEOPLE, Hernandez sometimes drove at night during periods of extreme heat, adjusted her son's anti-seizure medication schedule and dressed him in moisture-wicking clothes during the two-hour drives to his medical appointments.Buying another vehicle had not been financially possible, particularly after the air conditioning in the family's mobile home also broke down.Hernandez was secretly nominated by her brother, who had started a charity after losing his son in an ATV accident. When King eventually met her and presented her with a check, she was stunned.“Things like this don't happen to me,” Hernandez told PEOPLE. “I was completely shocked.”She said King's gesture made her feel heard and valued.“He made me feel important, that even though I have these obstacles in my life, I still matter,” she said.Another family receives $10,000The team also helped Maci Johnson, 30, and her husband Justin, 37, in Hico, Texas.The couple's 1-year-old son, Carter, was born with only a small portion of a fibula. After consulting several doctors, they were told he would either require multiple surgeries throughout childhood or undergo an amputation of his foot and ankle.The family ultimately chose amputation.Medical expenses, travel for appointments and hotel bills had put additional financial pressure on the family. Johnson, a speech therapist, had reduced her working hours to part-time to accommodate medical appointments, some of which required two-hour drives to Dallas.The family lives in a tiny house that does not have a bedroom for Carter and has limited space for mobility equipment he may eventually need.When the Johnsons were told they had been selected to receive financial support from the Gobundance Foundation, they initially thought it was a scam.King and his team eventually arrived on bicycles and presented the family with a $10,000 check.Johnson said the money could help them put a down payment on a larger home.“It helps give us that silver lining back,” she said. “There’s a light at the end of the tunnel. There’s hope for us to provide better for our kids.”More than $766,000 raisedBy the end of the ride, King had raised more than $766,000, with the total continuing to increase. The money has been distributed among more than 70 individuals and organisations, with individual gifts ranging from $100 to $75,000.One of King's favourite stops came at Daisy Mae’s Cafe in Arkansas City, Kansas, where locals had gathered for breakfast on a rainy morning after taking a break from working in the fields.King and his team bought breakfast for the entire diner and gave $200 tips to the wait staff.During the stop, one of the crew members also met a local man named Chris, who had lost his home in an electrical fire the previous year. King said Chris and his wife needed $36,000 but were unable to qualify for a new loan.The team decided to help.'We get to' make a differenceThe journey ultimately took 12 days rather than the planned 13.Reflecting on the experience, King said his biggest lesson was the impact that can come from simply taking time to listen to people.“We're showing up in communities that are often overlooked and we're helping people in need. They're good, amazing human beings,” he said.King added that many recipients told him the team did not need to help them.“My response is always the same, ‘I know we don't need to, but we get to,’” he said.Although the physical challenge is over, King says his efforts are far from finished. He is already planning a larger initiative for next year.“The Gobundance Foundation is going to keep doing things to help people in small towns, not just here in America, but worldwide,” King said. “What I really felt at the finish line is I felt like my job wasn't done yet.”You use AI every day. FOX 5 in Las Vegas reported that Jennifer Ortiz and Magdellena Romero were arrested after the Sept. 30 confrontation outside Planet Hollywood, where officers responded to reports of a fight involving women dressed in showgirl costumes. The altercation began when two visitors from North Carolina stopped to take pictures with three women dressed as showgirls in exchange for a tip, according to an arrest report reviewed by the station. CUSTOMERS HIT WITH AUTOMATIC 20% GRATUITIES AS RESTAURANTS COMBAT TIPPING CONFUSION After paying $20, the tourists began walking away when Ortiz allegedly followed them and demanded between $60 and $180 for the photos. articles.title: In 2007, Bryan Cranston bought a California beach bungalow for $2.5 million; after rebuilding it as a 2,450-sq-ft net-zero energy home, he sold the property 14 years later for $5.45 million
articles.summary: In 2007, actor Bryan Cranston, who is best know for playing Walter White in hit TV series 'Breaking Bad', purchased a modest beach bungalow in Venice,
articles.body: In 2007, actor Bryan Cranston, who is best know for playing Walter White in hit TV series 'Breaking Bad', purchased a modest beach bungalow in Venice, California, for $2.5 million, drawn by the location just steps from the sand. Rather than simply renovating the existing structure, he tore it down and rebuilt it as a 2,450-square-foot net-zero energy home designed to produce as much energy as it consumes. Fourteen years later, in 2021, he sold the property for $5.45 million, reflecting both the premium for beachfront land in Venice and the added value of a high-performance, eco-friendly residence, according to Realtor.com and a PR Newswire listing announcement. Read more details about it here:From bungalow to net-zero beach houseThe original property was a small, older beach bungalow typical of the Venice shoreline, where many homes were built decades ago with limited attention to energy efficiency. Cranston’s decision to rebuild allowed him to start from scratch and incorporate modern sustainable design from the foundation up. The new house was conceived not just as a luxury home but as a statement about what residential construction could achieve in terms of environmental performance.The finished home totals about 2,450 square feet of living space, a size that balances comfort with efficiency. The design features clean lines and natural materials, reflecting the relaxed yet refined esthetic of coastal California living. It includes multiple bedrooms and bathrooms, open living areas, and large windows that allow natural light and views of the surrounding neighborhood and nearby beach. Achieving net-zero energy status required careful consideration of insulation, air sealing, mechanical systems, and on-site power generation. The house was built to minimise heat loss in winter and heat gain in summer, reducing the load on heating and cooling systems. Solar panels and other renewable energy features were integrated into the design so that the home could generate enough electricity over the course of a year to offset its consumption, as per the reports.Cranston’s rebuild went beyond standard green upgrades. The home was designed with a focus on reducing its carbon footprint across multiple dimensions, including energy use, water consumption and material selection.According to an ET report, the house eventually earned LEED Platinum status, the highest tier awarded by the U.S. Green Building Council above Certified, Silver, and Gold. Rather than relying solely on the U.S. Department of Energy’s standard 'Zero Energy Ready Home' designation, calling Cranston’s residence a net-zero carbon footprint home paints a far more accurate picture of the build. Back when constructing sustainable custom houses was still nowhere near mainstream, this project served as a powerful real-world example of what energy-efficient residential design could truly accomplish.A home shaped by location and lifestyleVenice Beach is one of the most desirable and expensive neighbourhoods in Los Angeles, known for its boardwalk, artistic community and proximity to the ocean. Homes in this area typically command a hefty premium for owning a home just steps from the sand, and often attract buyers who appreciate both lifestyle and investment potential. Cranston’s purchase in 2007 came before the full run-up in prices that followed in subsequent years, giving him a favourable entry point.The net-zero rebuild allowed him to maximise the value of that location. A standard renovation might have improved the bungalow’s comfort and appearance, but a complete reconstruction offered the chance to create a home that matched contemporary expectations for performance and sustainability. For buyers interested in eco-friendly features, the property stood out in a market where many beach homes are older and less efficient.Talking about the house, Cranston said in a press statement, “I put my heart, soul, and blood, sweat, and often tears into it, and I’m glad, because it was such an artistic endeavor, and yet functional... There’s something lovely about creating something with tremendous pride and effort and turning it over… letting someone else take it to the next level of appreciation.”From listing to saleCranston listed the home in early 2021 with an asking price of $4.995 million, marketing it as a beachfront net-zero carbon footprint residence. The listing highlighted the home’s sustainable features, its location near the beach and its modern design, positioning it as a rare combination of eco-performance and coastal lifestyle. The property drew attention from buyers interested in both the environmental credentials and the Venice address.The home ultimately sold for $5.45 million, above the original asking price, reflecting strong demand for high-quality beachfront properties in Los Angeles. The sale price represented a gain of about $2.95 million over Cranston’s 2007 purchase price of $2.5 million, though it does not account for the costs of demolition, reconstruction and 14 years of ownership. Even so, the transaction demonstrates that sustainable features can add tangible value in a competitive market.For the buyer, the purchase offered a move-in-ready net-zero home in one of the city’s most sought-after neighbourhoods. For Cranston, the sale marked the end of a long-term project that began with a modest bungalow and ended with a showcase of what a modern beach house can be. The property’s transformation from old house to high-performance home is a case study in the positive effects of thoughtful rebuilding on environmental impact and market value.You use AI every day. articles.summary: NEW DELHI: A group of 42 retired judges on Thursday slammed the opposition's attack on Election Commission, claiming that it appeared to be a calculated
articles.body: NEW DELHI: A group of 42 retired judges on Thursday slammed the opposition's attack on Election Commission, claiming that it appeared to be a calculated campaign driven by "vested political interests" with little regard for the potentially devastating consequences of destabilising the world's largest democracy."India's constitutional bodies are under sustained attack. EC stands at the centre of this assault. Even the higher judiciary, which we hold in high esteem, and statutory agencies have not been spared. These attacks are not reasoned critique," they said in an open letter.Former Supreme Court judges Hemant Gupta and Pankaj Mittal and several former chief justices of high courts, besides retired judges of various HCs were signatories to the statement, which defended the EC's Special Intensive Review (SIR) of electoral rolls, arguing that a clean roll protected every genuine vote.They said they held no brief for any political party but in moments like these, silence was no longer a neutral choice. Constitutional authorities were now branded "thieves", "puppets" and "compromised" from public platforms, they said in a reference to EC's sharp criticism by opposition functionaries and organisations like CJP.Targeting Congress, they said: "EVMs are blamed only after defeat. Victories won on the same machines go unquestioned. A party that governed this nation for over five decades now claims that the very system which elected it is rigged."They said activist outfits with a long record of selective litigation lent these claims a veneer of legality. "They file petitions one after the other. They seldom file proof. The courtroom becomes a stage, and when the judgement is delivered, it is criticised whenever it does not serve their interests."The uproar over SIR appeared both sudden and remarkably convenient, the judges said. "Tell citizens often enough that their vote does not count, and they stop believing in the ballot. When the ballot loses meaning, the street gains it. Unrest begins with a narrative. Anarchic and fringe elements then occupy the vacuum," the group said.While some of these groups were homegrown, some took their cues from beyond borders, they alleged. articles.title: Putin pledges Russia’s support to end US-led war on Iran
articles.summary: The Russian and Iranian presidents met in Turkmenistan ahead of regional summit.
articles.body:
Russian President Vladimir Putin has told Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian that Russia will “do everything” to help end the United States-led war on Iran, Russian news agencies reported.

The two leaders met in Turkmenistan on Thursday ahead of the summit of the Commonwealth of Independent States, a group of former Soviet nations.

“You know our position. On our part, we are ready to do everything we can to help you resolve this situation,” Interfax news agency said Putin told Pezeshkian.

“We know that Iran is making real efforts to end the conflict, which broke out through no fault of its own, no fault of Iran’s,” Putin said, according to Russian media.

Putin also noted what he called a “positive evolution” in Iran-Russia relations.

In a call on Wednesday, Putin told Pezeshkian that Moscow is prepared to mediate efforts to end the war in the Middle East, Iran’s IRNA news agency reported.

Putin and Pezeshkian also met on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit in Kyrgyzstan last month.

The two countries, which are under heavy Western sanctions, have reinforced diplomatic and military ties.

Last year, Moscow and Tehran signed a “comprehensive strategic partnership treaty” that covers areas from trade and military cooperation to science, culture and education.

Ukraine and Western countries have accused Iran of supplying Russia with Shahed drones and short-range missiles for use in the Ukraine war. Russia has also been accused of supplying data to Iran for its attacks on US targets in the Middle East.

The meeting came as Iran-US talks stand at an apparent impasse.

US President Donald Trump said on Thursday that the US will not launch an attack on Iran before the November 3 US midterm congressional elections, saying the two countries are ‌‌holding “productive” talks about ending the ongoing war.

Diplomatic efforts to resolve Russia’s offensive in Ukraine also appear deadlocked, even as both sides intensify attacks.

articles.title: Iranian protester hanged hours after marrying his imprisoned fiancée over jail phone line
articles.summary: Alireza Sepahi married his imprisoned fiancée over a prison phone line hours before his execution at Isfahan Central Prison for anti-government protest.
articles.body: An Iranian anti-regime protester was hanged at dawn Oct. 5 inside Isfahan Central Prison, just hours after marrying his imprisoned fiancée over a jail phone line, The Times reported Thursday. Alireza Sepahi, 25, was executed alongside co-defendant Alireza Raisi after being sentenced to death in the anti-government demonstrations at Isfahan’s Alikhani Square Jan. 8., according to Human Rights Iran. Sepahi and his bride, student activist Mahshad Keshani, 22, knew and loved each other before being arrested during anti-regime demonstrations, the report said. IRAN HANGS 2 PROTESTERS IN PUBLIC, CROWD CRIES 'DISHONORABLE' AS SECURITY FIRES TEAR GAS Keshani, who is serving a five-year sentence, pushed for an informal wedding Sunday as fears mounted that Sepahi’s execution was imminent after a final family summons. The couple exchanged vows over the phone from inside Isfahan prison, joined by their fathers. Human rights lawyer Amirsalar Davoudi facilitated the ceremony by reading the vows for the fathers to bless. Keshani’s family gave a copy of the Quran, a saffron rock candy and a single red rose as a traditional dowry. "It was Mahshad’s idea," Davoudi told The Times. "Even now, I wonder how one young woman can possess such courage." IRAN TO EXECUTE FIRST FEMALE PROTESTER TIED TO ANTI-REGIME UNREST Davoudi recalled warning Keshani about the permanent nature of the decision. "I told her, ‘My dear, you understand that this cannot simply be undone?’" Davoudi said. "She said, ‘Mr Davoudi, I love Alireza.’" When Davoudi presented the proposal to Sepahi, the young man broke down in tears. "Alireza was crying, and something deeply painful and beautiful happened. Even the prison officers began to cry," Davoudi said. The ceremony held no formal authority to halt the execution. Sepahi had previously survived a scheduled hanging in July after suffering a heart attack on his way to the gallows. Authorities then rescheduled the execution after he regained consciousness. On Monday morning, hours after the vows were spoken, Sepahi was hanged. IRAN'S REGIME CAME FOR TEENAGE TWINS. THEIR FATE OFFERS A GLIMPSE OF TEHRAN'S WIDENING DEATH CAMPAIGN He is among seven defendants executed in the Alikhani Square case, in which 12 men were accused in the deaths of four security personnel. After the hanging, Sepahi’s family was reportedly prevented by authorities from burying their son in his hometown. Davoudi condemned the Iranian regime's actions. "I do not know how to come to terms with this," Davoudi said. "The regime is taking revenge on innocent young people for the humiliation it has suffered internationally." Human rights groups report Keshani remains in custody, facing additional security charges. This came as Maryam Rajavi, president-elect of the National Council of Resistance of Iran (NCRI), urged U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres to take immediate international action to halt executions and the killing of protesters in Iran, citing thousands of executions and decades of impunity for human rights abuses. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP In a letter ahead of World Day Against the Death Penalty on Oct. 10, Rajavi called for international accountability, independent investigations and diplomatic and economic pressure on Tehran to end the executions.

articles.title: ADHD and autism at risk of over-diagnosis, says government review
articles.summary: The review, which focuses on younger people, warned there was a risk society was moving from an era of under-diagnosis to over-diagnosis.
articles.body:
There is a risk of people being over-diagnosed with ADHD and autism, an official review in England has found.

Experts said a rise in diagnoses over the past 25 years meant cases now appear to be outstripping the expected number in the population for some younger age groups.

The review called for tougher regulation of private firms offering assessments for the NHS, saying they had concerns about quality and consistency, and a ban on advertising.

It concluded economic uncertainty combined with social media was driving an increase in mental health problems among young people and said there needed to be better support in place for all conditions.

The review - led by leading doctors in the field - was ordered 10 months ago by Wes Streeting after the then-health secretary claimed in an interview that young people were over-diagnosed and "written off".

It looked at people of all ages, but particularly focused on young people and children who have the highest rates of diagnoses.

It is likely to feed into government policies on everything from NHS services and benefits to support for young people who are not in education, employment or training.

The experts said too often diagnoses of mental health problems and ADHD and autism were ending up as labels that defined people by their "difficulties rather than their strengths and potential", harming their prospects at school, in work and in relationships.

Children diagnosed with autism and ADHD before the age of 17 are around four times more likely to end up not in education, employment or training between 16 and 24.

With better support after diagnosis, they could be helped to live more fulfilling lives, the review said.

Alongside access to therapies, this should also include support for mental health – significant numbers also struggle with conditions such as depression.

But the review found people were also being harmed by long waits for diagnosis for mental health and ADHD and autism.

The Watsons are just one family who have experience of this. Ryan and his wife knew there was something different with their son Atlas when he was around 12 to 18 months old and missing development milestones.

But it took three years to get an autism assessment. As time passed, his needs became increasingly clear. Now nearly seven, Atlas is non-verbal, still wears nappies and relies on others for all aspects of daily care.

Despite this, Ryan said there was no fast-track route for children with the most complex needs. "You basically go on the list and wait however long until you get to the top."

The wait left the family racing against time to secure support before Atlas started school. Ryan and his wife feared he would be placed in a mainstream school.

"We were terrified," Ryan says. "Anyone who has a child like Atlas will have the same panic that they'll start in a mainstream school where it's not safe."

The strain was immense. "It was like I had two jobs," Ryan says. "I was going to work and then coming home and dealing with these things."

Atlas was eventually diagnosed only months before starting school.

To ensure families like the Watsons get quicker assessment, the review calls for reassessment of those on waiting lists to ensure people with the highest needs are prioritised first and to look at whether some could be removed and offered other kinds of non-medical support.

This could include adjustments being made at school or in workplaces and lifestyle support, such as help to improve sleep or address anxiety, it said.

Too often, access to help requires a diagnosis, with experts highlighting changes in 2014 that required parents to get a diagnosis of autism and ADHD to qualify their children for extra support in schools.

Review chair Prof Peter Fonagy said it was clear the system was "under immense strain" and it was time to get away from diagnosis being a "very narrow pathway" to finding support.

"Diagnosis remains essential and must be protected - what has to change is that it is no longer the only door through which help can be reached."

Successive governments 'have failed autistic people'

The review said not every difficulty required a medical response and there was a risk of blurring the lines between diagnosable ADHD and autism and what should be considered the normal human variation in brain function, cognition and behaviour.

It said there was a risk society was now moving from an era of under-diagnosis to over-diagnosis or mis-diagnosis, pointing to data showing more than 4% of children aged six to 17 were now diagnosed with autism, well above the 1-2% that studies suggest is the true level.

But it said because some of these figures date back nearly a decade it was not possible to be absolutely certain or conclude over-diagnosis was currently occurring at scale.

Mel Merritt, of the National Autistic Society, said the report shows that successive governments "have failed autistic people".

"The harm and distress autistic people are facing is real and widespread and there is a desperate need to build a system that supports the needs of autistic people."

Abigail Ampofo, of charity YoungMinds, said: "For years, young people have told us they feel blamed for their mental health or accused of making it up. We hope this review goes some way to show them their distress is not their fault and the systems around them are failing."

But she said that would require major reform.

The government welcomed the publication of the report and said it would be setting out a new model of providing support in its forthcoming mental health strategy, which is expected before the end of the year, and also promised to introduce tougher regulation of ADHD and autism assessments.

Health Secretary Yvette Cooper added: "Professor Fonagy's review has shown the importance of early intervention to address mental health and neurodevelopmental conditions and the huge distress these can cause."

articles.title: 'Add me to WhatsApp' scam calls to be investigated
articles.summary: The UK's data watchdog is investigating a spike in complaints about "robo calls" that appear to lead to a recruitment scam.
articles.body:
The UK's data watchdog is investigating a spike in complaints about "robo calls" - where a recorded voice asks you to add them on WhatsApp - that are suspected to lead to a recruitment scam.

The Information Commission's Office (ICO) had more than 3,600 complaints about automated calls in September - a five-year high and nearly three times the number it had in July.

But it suspects millions of people are getting these calls and told BBC Radio 4's You and Yours it was "deeply concerned" by the sharp rise.

The ICO advises people to ignore calls from numbers they don't recognise, and to block and report any suspicious calls to the watchdog.

The automated calls typically come from what appears to be a UK mobile number.

Some of the recorded messages mention an offer of part-time work.

Simon Fell, from the Communications Crime Strategy Group, a telecoms industry body set up to tackle fraud, said he couldn't be sure exactly what form the scam would take as he hadn't followed up on the messages.

"Mostly likely it would be a recruitment scam ," he said.

"They would either put you through to a fake job listing, which might involve some form of money muling. It could look like a completely legitimate job, or something ad hoc, but they might pass criminal funds through your account which can lead to terrible consequences.

"It could also be a simple phishing exercise - criminals send out these messages, and what they really want to know is who's picking up, who's active - that information can be resold on the dark web.

"The possibilities are endless. At the end of the day this is a criminal that has reached out to you and they're trying to defraud you in some way shape or form."

Andy Curry, the ICO's head of criminal investigations, told the BBC he believed the calls were coming from abroad.

"We are trying to find who is behind this, why they're doing it and the impact it's having on members of the public," he said.

The number of complaints received by the ICO would only be a small proportion of the totals affected, he said.

"We think there are probably millions of people who are receiving these messages, which appear to us to be largely indiscriminate.

"I've had them, my colleague who's leading the investigation has had them. It's likely to be tip of the iceberg."

'I lost my savings after a job interview scam'

Rise in reports of 'shameful' recruitment scams

Fell said that mobile companies were "working on a range of fronts" to tackle the influx of automated calls.

This includes sending intelligence reports to the regulator Ofcom, working with law enforcement, and liaising with Meta, which owns WhatsApp, because if someone does follow up on the request to add the number to the encrypted platform, "any dialogue that happens between you and the criminal then can't be investigated any further".

A WhatsApp spokesman said there were features in place to protect its users from scam calls, including silencing calls from unknown numbers. He also said WhatsApp banned millions of accounts each year for "malicious behaviours", such as bulk account registration or automated messaging.

While these calls typically appear to be from a UK mobile number, Fell said these numbers will be imitated, or spoofed, by the criminals behind the scam.

Last November, the UK government promised that call spoofing would be eliminated within a year.

A Home Office spokesman said the government was taking "robust action" to tackle scams.

"We remain committed to delivering the Telecommunications Charter, alongside industry, by November," he added.

articles.title: Celebrity Traitors episode three: Emotions run high as two players banished
articles.summary: Viewers watched to see whether Richard E Grant could save himself at the first round table of the series.
articles.body:
Spoiler warning: This article reveals details from the third episode of The Celebrity Traitors, series two.

We normally expect raised voices, conflicting theories and a dramatic showdown from the Celebrity Traitors. But as this year's first round table got under way, the writing was on the castle wall.

Viewers who often get frustrated with the faithful and root for them to uncover a traitor had their wish firmly Richard E Grant-ed on Thursday, as the actor was banished in a landslide vote.

His questionable strategy of revealing he was a traitor to the other celebrities in the bar led to the first time in the UK version of the show that a traitor has been identified at the opening round table.

"Thank you for giving me an almost bingo full-house of votes," Grant told his fellow players. "I have always wanted to be a traitor, and sometimes in life your dreams do come true."

There was jubilation from the other celebrities as Grant confirmed his identity, waving his hands in the air. Ross Kemp was so happy it came out as borderline anger, with a vein-popping "get in there!"

Other players seemed genuinely shocked. "This is me with men all the time," joked comedian Joanne McNally, who hadn't voted for Grant. "I completely believed him!"

But although the faithful had successfully found a traitor, and even managed to spell his name correctly on their slates, the first round table saw some other players behave in ways that immediately aroused suspicion.

Julie Hesmondhalgh noticed Myha'la ostentatiously winking at Grant before she voted for him, which later prompted the former Coronation Street actress to make one of the most impassioned - but mistaken - speeches of the night.

"It was traitor-on-traitor," she declared (it wasn't). "I don't know if anybody else saw it," (we did). "I am so excited because I truly believe we can get two in a row," (don't count on it).

The remaining traitors, Maya Jama and James Acaster, met in the turret later with the choice of murdering previously shortlisted players Jerry Hall and Hannah Fry, or seducing a third traitor to replace Grant.

The pair ultimately decided to recruit mathematician Fry, who had the most wonderful and meme-able reaction when she found out that, not only was she not being murdered, she was being seduced.

Accepting the offer, Fry joined Jama and Acaster in the turret, exclaiming as she learned their identities: "I had both of you down as faithful!"

The new trio discussed how they would approach breakfast the next morning, before Acaster delivered the line of the episode.

"It's changing a lot, this Traitors," he observed of the fluid line-up. "It's like the Sugababes."

The next morning, there were shocked faces when the players realised everybody had made it to breakfast unscathed, with the celebrities concluding that one player must have been recruited.

"It was fascinating seeing Jerry and Hannah come back," said Miranda Hart. "Hannah seemed different, as if something new has happened to her." Oh yes? "I definitely clocked a nervousness in her, which is very interesting."

We could have a first-rate traitor hunter on our hands here. But would any of Hart's fellow players feel the same way? "Poor Hannah," said McNally, "she's been recruited." Uh-oh.

As the theories continued to float around across various sub-meetings, with Hesmondhalgh, Bella Ramsey and several others setting their sights on Myha'la, the celebrities headed out to the next mission.

Presenter Claudia Winkleman explained the latest task would see them use a battering ram to break down the doors of four crypts, where they could find money to add to the prize pot - and also potentially bag some shields.

James Blunt immediately took control, assigning players various roles. "He was full army officer," Hart observed. "I found it mildly erotic."

"I don't think I've ever used a battering ram," Joe Lycett reflected. "I would use a battering ram to get into [Wicked star] Jonathan Bailey's house, but that's it."

Myha'la and Fry entered one crypt, found a shield and debated who should keep it. They agreed on Myha'la, partly because she had grabbed it first, although she sweetly suggested that the pair could keep it secret from the other players to protect both of them.

Jama and Sharon Rooney, meanwhile, scored two further shields, but the players then found that some shields would have to be given up anyway in order to unlock the final chest of prize money.

Rooney and Myha'la surrendered theirs, but traitor Jama quietly held on to hers. The other players didn't know she had one, and the TV presenter asked Rooney to keep it secret. That decision could come back to bite her in later episodes.

In the cars on the way back, the players continued to debate various hunches, with one particularly awkward journey where Myha'la and Hesmondhalgh admitted they were suspicious of each other.

"I feel like you've been a little bit vague," said Hesmondhalgh. "That's only because I've thought it's been you from day one," Myha'la replied.

We've certainly come a long way from the pair's first exchange just two episodes ago. "It's lovely to meet you Myha'la, I'm such a big fan!" - "Oh my God, thank you!"

Back in the castle, Rob Beckett had adopted a new policy. "When someone comes up to talk to me, I just agree with them, whatever they say," he laughed in the castle's diary room.

As the players gathered for the second banishment of the episode, discussion inevitably turned to prime suspect Myha'la.

"I've heard my name a whole bunch today," she acknowledged, as the others struggled to square her behaviour during the mission.

The actress became visibly emotional as she recounted the events of the crypt and attempted to justify grabbing the shield before offering it to Fry.

"I was going to give it to her," Myha'la said tearfully. "I was worried about my protection, but I thought maybe [Fry] had more heat."

Sensing that the tide was turning against Myha'la, Fry stuck the knife in. "Why would you scrabble for the shield, and then be keen to give it away?" she asked.

Despite a sprinkling of votes for other players, Myha'la became the second casualty of the episode. "I have loved getting to know you all," she said as she confirmed her faithful status to the other players.

Hart became even more suspicious of Fry, however, after realising the mathematician had orchestrated events to make Myha'la's behaviour at the crypt look less innocent. "Miss Marple is so on," Hart said with a smile.

Later, the traitors met in the turret and debated who their next victim should be, settling on a shortlist of Blunt, Ramsey and Sebastian Croft.

Acaster had a characteristically unique reason for suggesting James Blunt.

"It would make my life easier," he said, "because every time someone says 'James', I'm turning around, and half the time, it's for him."

articles.title: Why are more roofs not made of solar tiles?
articles.summary: Solar tiles were touted as an attractive alternative to solar panels - why have they not taken off?
articles.body:
Some people in the US "still hate the look of solar", Kate Collardson acknowledges.

She would know. Collardson handles operations for the Solar Service of Colorado, a solar maintenance and inspection company. She's also held just about every other job in the industry, from installer to instructor.

For those that hate the look of solar panels, an alternative is a solar roof, where the tiles (or shingles) house solar cells, but look much the same as regular tiles.

This is especially important for historic buildings, where heritage rules limit changes to their appearance.

For many people, the first time they'd heard of this product category was in August, when Tesla's website stopped offering solar roofs . This followed disappointing sales and a lawsuit over sudden price hikes .

Other companies have also pulled out, but Tesla's decision in particular sent shockwaves through the solar roof industry.

Some see it as a death knell for solar tiles; others, as an opportunity.

For instance, the small Swiss company Freesuns is considering expanding to the US.

Deborah Learoyd, Freesuns' CEO and managing director, estimates that the company's sales have grown 20–30% since it was established in 2019.

In general, solar roof components continue to be manufactured in smaller batches. This limits the economies of scale and standardisation, though flexible manufacturing could help somewhat.

Learoyd says that while the unit costs for Freesuns' products are slowly decreasing, "a lot of the cost is actually the fact that every roof is a little bit different. And so it has to be engineered a little bit differently, installed a little bit differently".

Solar roofs typically require collaboration among roofers, solar installers and electricians. And building regulations tend to be more complex than for solar panels.

The additional time and paperwork can take a toll on a roofing business, Collardson explains. "You try to put a roofer into the equation and they're going, 'This is taking forever. I'm losing money. I could have sold 10 roofing jobs in the time that it takes me to sell this one'."

Collardson has to charge more for repair of solar shingles, compared to a standard photovoltaic (PV) setup.

She explains, "With traditional solar, we generally have electronics on the panel and a map that shows us exactly how much each panel is producing." So when something goes wrong, it's easy to spot where.

"With solar shingles, we don't really have the benefit of that mapping; there's no room underneath the shingle for the electronics." Thermal cameras can identify the trouble spots, however.

But then there's the matter of accessing them. "You can remove the one in the middle of the array, but you have to walk on the others, and you really shouldn't walk on them because you're going to create micro-fractures and that's going to cause issues down the road."

Before repair costs are factored in, a solar roof might cost twice as much as a system of solar panels mounted on a roof.

Solar roofs are also less efficient - one reason is that the tiles are just smaller.

Another factor is the energy lost as heat. Since the tiles sit close to the roof, there's less airflow than with standard solar panels mounted on a roof. Heat impairs solar performance.

Coloured tiles are even less efficient, comments Ben Graves, co-founder of UK solar company Sunsave. "The reason why all solar cells are black, and increasingly the whole panel is now black, is because black is the best absorbing colour."

Overall, much more space would need to be devoted to solar roof tiles to produce the same amount of energy.

Sunsave does not offer solar roofs. "Most people in the UK just don't have enough money to pay for it," Graves believes.

While appearance was a bigger factor five years ago, now "the vast majority of consumers are most interested in how much they can save".

But supporters of solar roofs argue that they should not be pitted against standard solar modules on roofs.

"Let's not compare PV roof tiles to a standard PV system, but look at PV roof tiles as generating additional electricity from our roofs instead of just having the roof sit there," urges Martin Heinrich who leads a research group at the Fraunhofer Institute for Solar Energy Systems in Germany.

While standard solar panels have gone from strength to strength, solar roofs have not advanced to the same extent.

One advancement that could especially help solar roofs is matrix shingling technology.

This is a different way of connecting solar cells. The solar cells are cut into narrow strips, layered like overlapping shingles, and connected to each other using electrically conductive adhesive, rather than metal wires.

This means that the electrical current can flow around shaded areas, unlike with standard modules. "If you get like a bird pooping on a part of the cell, the current can go around it," Learoyd explains.

In addition to increasing energy output, this improves the appearance as the silver wires aren't visible.

Another advantage, Heinrich says, is that "since we cut the cells into smaller areas, we can fill out special sizes more easily. You don't have to adhere to the regular pattern size."

Freesuns is an early adopter of matrix shingling technology in building-integrated PV. "We see it as a big opportunity for the future in terms of how we would make our tiles," Learoyd says.

What would also help the company is better software for automated design. This would speed up the design process, since each roofing job is unique.

Learoyd believes this would lower costs and give "the whole construction industry much more confidence in using the product".

Ten years after her own solar roof was installed, and despite the sector's setbacks, Learoyd remains optimistic.

She believes that for people with the means, it will eventually become standard to install a new roof with some sort of embedded solar. "It's just a no-brainer."

articles.title: Zuckerberg's image is in trouble - but Meta's business is booming
articles.summary: A new film paints the Meta founder as a villain. But the tech firm seems immune to bad publicity, writes our North America tech correspondent.
articles.body:
Mark Zuckerberg was just three minutes into his keynote speech at the company's annual Meta Connect product event last month when his tone turned almost wistful.

"Building is an act of love," he said, glancing down at the ground with his hands in his pockets. "It's how we impart what we believe, and we pour our hearts and our souls into what we make."

Speaking to hundreds of analysts and developers, Zuckerberg proceeded to share news about Meta's latest AI products: its new agentic chatbot Muse, a slew of smart glasses, as well as a Tamagotchi-like AI gadget users can attach to their wrists.

It was a conference focused on new technologies - but still, it's perhaps notable that during a presentation lasting nearly an hour, Zuckerberg did not mention two of his most popular products, Instagram and Facebook, the social media platforms that have helped Meta become a $2tn company.

For much of the past year, Meta has been embroiled in a series of legal actions, accused of deliberately designing products that are addictive to young users.

That has led to the release of internal emails, corporate documents and whistleblower testimony that personal injury lawyers and prosecutors across the country have wielded to make their case.

And Zuckerberg is unpopular: last year, a Pew Research Center poll found that two-thirds of Americans had an unfavourable opinion of him.

His reputation is unlikely to be helped by The Social Reckoning, a film by Aaron Sorkin released this week. It's about whistleblower claims that Meta executives were aware of their products harming young people. Succession actor Jeremy Strong plays Zuckerberg as a "full-on villain", according to a review in the Hollywood Reporter, "stoically arguing that even the slightest gesture of responsibility is anathema where money is concerned".

Some speculate that this is Meta's "Big Tobacco" moment, with a consensus forming against the company, and the social media industry as a whole.

But the truth seems to be more complicated. Despite months of bad press, in the real world Meta's products are doing better than ever. Use of its apps continues to rise, and users are already flocking to its new AI assistant.

It raises the question: can anything really clip Meta's wings? Or is it now something of a 'Teflon' company, with scandals simply bouncing off it?

It's certainly been a year of bad headlines for Meta.

Last summer, Reuters revealed that Meta allowed its chatbots to "engage a child in conversations that are romantic or sensual", and provide false medical information to users.

Meta has revised those policies and said that such responses should never have been allowed.

And this year, bills have been mounting. In March, a jury gave $6m (£4.5m) to a 20-year-old California woman who claimed she suffered mental health harms related to her use of Meta's Instagram and Google's YouTube.

Around the same time, New Mexico became the first state to succeed in a lawsuit against Meta over child safety issues. A jury found the company had failed to warn the public about the dangers its platforms posed to kids. Meta was fined a total of $942m. The judge called Meta a "public nuisance" akin to air pollution.

Meta says it disagrees with the verdicts and is appealing both cases.

In May, Meta was among the social companies that avoided a trial by settling a case brought by a Kentucky school district that claimed their product design had led to a youth mental health crisis. Meta reportedly agreed to pay $9m, the most of any defendant.

And this summer, Meta struck a high-profile $18bn settlement with 48 US states, plus the District of Columbia and three US territories. Meta denied wrongdoing as part of the settlement, and during the five-day trial it maintained that it had worked extensively over the years to make its platforms safer for young users, pouring resources into testing and research. As part of the deal, the firm promised to enact two-hour daily time limits for young users, along with night-time blocks on use, muted notifications during school hours, and other changes.

The company faces other lawsuits too, including one starting later this month in Los Angeles, also related to alleged social media addiction among young users.

Meanwhile, several countries have moved to ban social media for children entirely, starting with Australia last December. Social media companies are broadly disliked, even while their products remain wildly popular. A Reuters/Ipsos survey suggests that 85% of Americans think social media can be addictive for children, and 61% support greater government oversight.

To some, the trust issue feels existential

"Once the public has stopped trusting you, it's kind of a downward spiral," says associate professor Alison Taylor of New York University's Stern School of Business.

"It feels like… the trust deficit is so big, I just don't know that they're going to be able to recover."

But despite those high-profile cases, the company reported that the number of people using some of its apps (like Instagram and WhatsApp) has risen 3% year on year and this year's second quarter revenue was up 28% compared with the same period in 2025.

While it has agreed to temper its pursuit of the teen market (which many brands eagerly cultivate to build their future user base), the company has said that teens accounted for less than 1% of its revenue anyway. Competitors TikTok and Google's YouTube are more popular with young users.

And the company's settlement with the 48 states was widely considered a massive win for Meta, because it prevented some Meta bosses (including Zuckerberg) from having to give testimony, and stopped the release of further internal documents, while allowing the company to avoid admitting wrongdoing. The company's stock price surged 4% immediately following the announcement, and is up more than 25% over the last month.

One view popular among critics is that the company has tested consumer tolerance for bad behaviour and until now, its business has mostly managed to withstand the blowback. In other words, people will continue to use the products even if they don't like the company.

"I think they're in a remarkably good position that I didn't expect them to be in," says Patrick Moorhead, founder and CEO of Moor Insights & Strategy.

However, Meta's move into AI depends partly on rebuilding public trust.

Last month, the company launched its new AI personal assistant app, Muse. Crucially, Muse is an AI agent, meaning it can carry out tasks in multiple stages and work on something over several hours (in contrast to chatbots like ChatGPT, which tend to do one task at a time).

It's the first AI agent from a major tech firm to become publicly available. A New York Times tech reporter who used the app for two weeks says he was "blown away"; the app called his dental insurer on his behalf, ordered him groceries and tracked his credit card spending in a spreadsheet.

But Muse works best when users hand over some of their most personal information to the company, including credit card information, purchase histories and access to email inboxes.

It's a big ask for a company whose reputation on privacy has been sullied, starting a decade ago with the Cambridge Analytica scandal, which followed the revelation that the data of millions of Facebook users was breached and used by a political consulting firm.

Just two days after Zuckerberg's keynote at Meta Connect, another New Mexico jury found Meta lied about how Facebook used personal information. (The company has said it disagrees with the verdict and will defend itself against what it says are efforts to distort its record.)

So are customers willing to hand over that data for the convenience of using Muse?

Some users say yes. Since its launch one month ago, Muse already has more than five million downloads and more than three million weekly active users - outpacing the adoption of ChatGPT when that was first introduced, in the North American market.

Zuckerberg has laid out a vision in which Muse couples with an ever-expanding line-up of Meta AI smart glasses, enabling users to summon hands-free what he calls "personal superintelligence".

Meta clearly has big plans for its smart glasses. "I think they're making an investment to position themselves as a category leader," says Kate Winick, principal analyst at Forrester, covering social media and influencers. "However big this category turns out to be, they will own it - for now."

The glasses are divisive, and have been labelled by some as "pervert glasses" because they can be used to film covertly. The company has moved to stop users from tampering with the light that indicates a photo or video is being captured. Zuckerberg also just announced new audio-only smart glasses, an apparent bid to quell privacy concerns.

But the company's most strident critics remain wary.

"Consumers know that Meta has problems, and that to date we haven't been able to trust them to make their products safe for children. So why would a consumer want to trust them with some of their most private and sensitive information?" says Brooke Istook of the Heat Initiative, a campaign group.

In his speech, Zuckerberg briefly addressed the sensitive issue of privacy. At one point during his talk, an image flashed on the screen behind him of its Muse mascot embracing a blue padlock.

"Given how personal Muse and the content on your glasses is, we designed state-of-the-art privacy and security into all these systems from the beginning," Zuckerberg told the audience.

He touted a personal virtual machine, for example - essentially a self-contained computer system running inside Meta's cloud, where it says Muse users' data will be stored. Zuckerberg promised it would keep every customer's information secure, and that soon "even Meta won't be able to see that information". He said the virtual machine will be launched later this year, with further privacy protections coming.

Meta's focus on privacy and security seems aimed at reassuring consumers. But Winick says users still have to opt into many of those protections. "I think if they thought they could get away with not doing that, they would," she says.

Not long after Zuckerberg took the stage in California, social media users started reporting cases of Muse running amok, including claims that the agent read emails without permission. Meta has pushed back against these reports, saying it does not believe that Muse accesses emails unless a user has consented.

In the end, the bulk of users may be willing to make some concessions on privacy if it means convenience and utility, says Moorhead. "If the consumer sees the trade-off as beneficial, then they'll keep it going," he says. "This is why Facebook and Instagram still have billions of users."

On the financial front, the social media advertising business – its cash cow – routinely brings in significant revenue. Meta reported $60.8bn in revenue and $15.9bn in profit for the second quarter of this year.

Consistent profits have helped fuel bets from the much-mocked Metaverse , to its current mass expansion of AI infrastructure.

And on Muse? "It's a very real time-saving benefit that a lot of people will want and will like," says Winick.

AI investment is not cheap. Meta has now taken on $83.7bn in long-term debt, according to its most recent financial statement.

Still, Meta executives are bullish about the company's pivot to AI. "It's really about your agent, who can do work on your behalf, who is your constant ally in whatever you're trying to accomplish in your goals in your life," Andrew Bosworth, the company's chief technology officer, said in an interview with the BBC.

Meta has big plans. But its future may ultimately depend on whether its users can trust it.

articles.title: Person shot by ICE officers in New York City
articles.summary: The person was apparently in a vehicle when at least one officer opened fire, according to a source.
articles.body: ICE officers shot a person Thursday afternoon in an Upper Manhattan neighborhood in New York, three law enforcement sources familiar with the matter said. The shooting happened around 4 p.m. during an ICE enforcement operation along Marble Hill Avenue, those sources said. One source said the person was apparently in a vehicle when at least one officer opened fire. That person was expected to survive. The Department of Homeland Security did not immediately respond to a request for comment Thursday. A massive law enforcement investigation surrounded a black sedan believed to be the vehicle where the person was shot. A senior official said a 5-year-old child was in the back seat at the time of the incident. New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani said that early reports indicate officers surrounded the man and a 5-year-old child in his car in the Marble Hill neighborhood and that the child was physically unharmed. Multiple law enforcement sources said the team of ICE officers was in the neighborhood looking for a man with a criminal record. A senior official said the suspect had a past robbery arrest resulting in a grand larceny conviction and a current open drug case. Homeland Security and the FBI are responding to the scene in addition to the New York Police Department, which confirmed the shooting by “federal law enforcement agents” on X. “The NYPD was not involved in the incident and was not on scene at the time of the shooting. The individual who was shot is at a nearby hospital and is currently conscious and receiving medical attention,” the NYPD said. Mamdani called the shooting “an unconscionable and incredibly serious situation” in a statement on X. “I have called the President; when we speak I will demand that he ends all ICE enforcement actions in our city. I will not stand by while ICE agents terrorize our communities,” he wrote. “Get ICE out of our neighborhoods. Get ICE out of our hospitals. Get ICE off our streets. Get ICE away from our children.” Gov. Kathy Hochul said that she had been briefed on the shooting and that she expected a detailed report from federal authorities about what happened. “We expect federal authorities to provide a full and transparent accounting of the circumstances surrounding this incident. New Yorkers deserve to know exactly what happened and why,” she wrote on X.

articles.title: Flydubai cockpit attack: Israel to honour Indian pilot Smit Machchhar with top civilian bravery award
articles.summary: Israel will honour Indian pilot Captain Smit Machchhar with the Presidential Award for Civil Heroism for his role in preventing a major aviation disaster
articles.body: Israel will honour Indian pilot Captain Smit Machchhar with the Presidential Award for Civil Heroism for his role in preventing a major aviation disaster aboard a flydubai flight bound for Tel Aviv, President Isaac Herzog announced on Thursday.Herzog made the announcement while presenting the Presidential Medal for Civilian Heroism to six Israeli passengers who helped thwart the alleged attempt to crash flight FZ1073 last week.The ceremony was held in Jerusalem.“Alongside the Israeli heroes we honor today, we send our heartfelt wishes for a full and speedy recovery to Captain Smit Machchhar of India. Captain Machchhar’s courage, bravery and professionalism helped prevent this catastrophe,” Herzog said.“Once he regains his strength, it will be an honour and a privilege for me to present him, on behalf of the people of Israel, with the Presidential State of Israel Award for Civil Heroism,” he added.The announcement came as Machchhar continued to recover in a hospital in Abu Dhabi after sustaining serious injuries during an alleged attack by his co-pilot inside the aircraft's cockpit.Six Israeli passengers honoured for thwarting attackHerzog presented the civilian heroism award to Tali Manes, Zvika Manes, Yaniv Hayoun, Dr Shota Musayev, Asaf Rajuan and Or Pardilov for their roles in preventing the alleged hijacking attempt, according to The Jerusalem Post and The Times of Israel.Tali Manes was credited with first raising the alarm, while Hayoun, Zvika Manes, Pardilov and Rajuan helped subdue the co-pilot after he allegedly attacked the captain. Musayev, a doctor, provided medical assistance to the injured pilot.“Today we gather in Jerusalem to honour six seemingly ordinary Israelis who proved to be extraordinary human beings, true heroes, by saving the flight last week,” Herzog said.“Thanks to their courage, determination and remarkable presence of mind, these heroes prevented a devastating aviation disaster that would have shocked the entire world and saved 174 precious lives.”The Israeli president also expressed gratitude to the replacement pilots who took over the aircraft and other passengers who helped during the emergency.Herzog said the passengers' actions could not remove the need for a full investigation into the incident.“The civilian bravery and resourcefulness demonstrated by the heroes gathered here cannot absolve us of the obligation to obtain full answers,” he said.What happened aboard the flydubai flight?The incident occurred last week aboard flydubai flight FZ1073, which was carrying 174 passengers to Israel. The co-pilot, identified as Omani national Hamam al-Hammami, allegedly attacked Machchhar with a crash axe inside the cockpit and attempted to take control of the aircraft.The aircraft transmitted emergency signals and made a rapid descent of more than 17,000 feet, from 34,000 feet, before making an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia. The UAE subsequently classified the incident as an attempted terrorist attack.Machchhar received initial treatment in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia, before being shifted to Abu Dhabi for further medical care.Ministry of external affairs said on Tuesday that the pilot was recovering well and responding positively to treatment. MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said the Indian embassy in the UAE was in regular contact with Machchhar, his family and hospital authorities.“Captain Smit Machchhar is in the hospital in Abu Dhabi. Our embassy in the UAE has been in regular touch with him, with his family, with local authorities, and with the hospital authorities. He's recuperating well. He's responding well. And his health is improving,” Jaiswal said.Netanyahu had invited pilot to Israel's Independence Day eventIsraeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had earlier spoken to Machchhar while he was receiving treatment in the UAE and praised his actions during the incident.Netanyahu invited the Indian pilot and Prime Minister Narendra Modi to light a flame at Israel's Independence Day event, describing Machchhar as a hero of Israel, India and the world.“It's our highest honour that we give on our Independence Day. It's usually reserved for Israeli citizens, but I think here in this case, all the citizens of Israel will embrace you. They do now, and they will then too. So we hope to see you very soon in Israel,” Netanyahu told the pilot.The Israeli president's announcement on Thursday means Machchhar will also receive a civilian heroism award once he has recovered sufficiently to travel.Herzog established the Presidential Medal for Civilian Heroism following the October 7, 2023, Hamas-led attack on Israel.The award recognises civilians who display extraordinary courage while putting themselves at genuine risk to save others.You use AI every day. articles.title: Huckabee aide suppressed US Embassy reports critical of Israeli government: Report
articles.summary: A top aide to Mike Huckabee, the U.S. ambassador to Israel, allegedly suppressed an embassy report that was critical of the Israeli government, according to The New York Times, which cited three U.S. officials who work with the aide. One of Huckabee’s senior advisors, David Milstein, reportedly quashed a memo that criticized Israel’s decision to…
articles.body:
A top aide to Mike Huckabee, the U.S. ambassador to Israel, allegedly suppressed an embassy report that was critical of the Israeli government, according to The New York Times , which cited three U.S. officials who work with the aide.

One of Huckabee’s senior advisors, David Milstein, reportedly quashed a memo that criticized Israel’s decision to approve more settlements in the Israeli-occupied West Bank, per the Times. Milstein allegedly blocked its release before it could be shared with Washington lawmakers.

He also reportedly insisted on approving communications from the U.S. Embassy sector that handled Palestinian affairs, according to multiple officials with direct knowledge of the matter. They said they spoke to the outlet out of concern that Milstein’s actions were undermining the standard of diplomatic work.

People who interacted with the aide continued that he went to “unusual lengths” to position Israel in a positive light, the publication reported.

According to his LinkedIn profile, Milstein previously worked as an aide to Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) and an adviser to Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis’s (R) gubernatorial campaign, where he handled “Jewish and pro-Israel outreach.”

In between his stints in both offices, Milstein worked as a special assistant to former U.S. Ambassador to Israel David Friedman during President Trump’s first term.

He also made headlines in September when he sent wedding invitations that asked for “monetary wedding gift[s]” in “U.S. dollars or Israeli shekels” alongside a QR code, according to screenshots reviewed by Politico’s Playbook .

Huckabee slammed this report, writing on social media , “If there is anyone I’ve worked with presently or over the past 50 years of my adult life which I’ve had absolute confidence in as one with impeccable integrity, it’s David Milstein.”

A source in the intelligence community reportedly told Politico, “[Milstein’s] a giant walking counterintelligence red flag … the fact that he is blatantly soliciting donations is absolutely jaw dropping.”

The Trump administration previously dropped sanctions against extremist Israeli settlers imposed by the Biden administration, though Huckabee has previously condemned Israeli settler violence in the West Bank, calling it an “act of terror.”

Huckabee has also criticized Americans’ rising dissatisfaction toward Israel, saying in an interview with The Hill’s broadcast partner, NewsNation, that both social media disinformation and foreign propaganda were behind much of this negative perception.

articles.title: 'I rage and I don't care': Why women are reclaiming their anger
articles.summary: Studies suggest women are getting angrier, but are they just more open about it?
articles.body:
Music artist Chess Galea used to suppress any feelings of anger, fearing she would be branded as "hysterical" or "difficult to work with".

From the "mental load" women carry to sexism in the workplace or - worse - violence against women, Galea says "we don't realise how much we accept and how much we close our mouths".

But now she says she simply lets it out: "If someone catcalls me in the street, I rage. I don't care."

Galea, 34, is one of an increasing number of women in the UK reporting feeling angrier than ever.

For nearly two decades, more women than men worldwide have reported experiencing daily anger, and the gap has been growing .

So are women actually feeling more anger - and what is driving that shift - or are they just more open about it?

It's a bit of both, suggests psychotherapist Jennifer Cox, author and co-host of the Women are Mad podcast.

She started researching anger after suspecting her female clients' suppression of it was the root cause of some of their physical conditions.

"There was this pattern of women coming in with migraines, stomach issues, musculoskeletal and immune issues. Ultimately it was hard to ignore," she says.

"They were trying to keep their kids on track, look after their mental health and somehow do their job [too]."

Cox later ran group sessions where many women let out pent-up feelings of anger.

"We've been brought up with this ridiculous 'good girl' stuff… indoctrinated in this idea of being good, polite, kind, thoughtful, caring," she says.

"The big change from previous generations is that we are expected to do it all."

While almost as many women work as men, they spend nearly an hour longer each day doing unpaid work such as chores or caring responsibilities, the Office for National Statistics says.

On top of that is the "mental load", the invisible labour of keeping a household running that often falls to women.

There are also more positive representations of angry women in the media.

Previously, characters like Alex Forrest (played by Glenn Close) in Fatal Attraction or Carrie (Sissy Spacek) in Stephen King's horror classic would often be portrayed as unstable and dangerous.

But today, female rage is increasingly positioned as understandable and even liberating.

Take Lily Allen's 2025 album West End Girl, which graphically documented the end of her marriage to actor David Harbour, as well as artists such as Charli XCX, Olivia Rodrigo and Chappell Roan releasing songs featuring violent imagery and even screams of rage.

On screen, even 2023's smash-hit Barbie showed the iconic doll expressing frustration with her supposedly picture-perfect world.

These depictions of women's anger are helpful and healthy, Cox says.

But when women act upon their anger in real life, they can face a social penalty.

A 2020 study found women expressing anger at work were seen as less deserving of status and influence, while their male counterparts were not.

So, can women express anger at work and still get ahead? Yes, says life coach Yann Dang, who specialises in coaching senior women in male-dominated fields.

Women who people-please and don't show negative emotion can progress to a certain level on the career ladder, but to make it to the top you need to rock the boat, she argues.

"Women are so good at learning the rules when we know what the rules are. But the rules in the corporate world are totally different."

The key, she says, is knowing how to harness your anger in a way that comes across as authentic.

Dang suggests women use direct language such as "That's a hard no for me"; "I don't like that"; and "I'm frustrated too." She also advises them to "build the muscle" of standing up for themselves, even if they don't have a perfectly polished response ready.

Alongside everyday sexism, ongoing threats including stalking, harassment and domestic abuse serve as powerful factors uniting women in anger and defiance.

Violence against women and girls accounts for nearly 20% of all recorded crime in England and Wales, but it often goes unreported.

For Galea, being able to discuss her experience of misogyny in the music industry as well as the sexual assault she was a victim of more openly with other women has helped to crystallise the frustration she feels.

"I think we've been angry for a long time but now we can access others because of social media," she says.

Psychologist Dr Tara Brach agrees anger has its place.

"The key thing is under anger there's something we care about. Anger is a messenger, it brings us energy to protect, confront injustices, set boundaries, to make a change.

"It becomes unhealthy when it possesses us, or when we act in ways that harm."

To channel it effectively, Brach advocates mindfulness, in particular the "RAIN" strategy - recognise the emotion, allow yourself to experience it, investigate the cause, and nurture feelings of understanding.

articles.title: Kenyan patient suspected of Ebola infection tests negative
articles.summary: Preliminary lab results ease fears of a second case in Kenya, after the country reported its first-ever case this week.
articles.body:
Preliminary laboratory results from a Kenyan patient who was suspected of contracting the Ebola virus have come back negative.

Fears of a second case of Ebola in the East African country were allayed on Thursday after the governor of Wajir County, where the patient is being treated, revealed the test results.

“I am pleased to report that the preliminary laboratory results indicate that the sample is NEGATIVE for Ebola Virus Disease,” the Wajir county governor said in a statement.

The suspected patient is a 20-year-old man with a travel history from the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) through Uganda to Kenya.

The other Kenyan patient who tested positive for the virus and subsequently died had travelled the same route.

Kenya had reported its first-ever Ebola case on Tuesday after a citizen who became sick in the DRC died in Nairobi.

The deadly strain of the Ebola virus has spread widely, starting in the DRC earlier this year. The DRC officially declared an outbreak in May.

Kenya is the fourth country to record a case linked to the Ebola epidemic in the DRC, the second-largest on record. The ongoing outbreak in the eastern DRC has killed at least 4,205 people out of more than 8,700 reported cases.

The outbreak spread across the border to Uganda, which had about 20 cases before being declared Ebola-free in July.

The strain behind the latest spread has been dubbed the Bundibugyo virus (BDBV), believed to have spread from animals to humans through a new transmission route. No vaccine currently exists for Bundibugyo.

The first case in Kenya drew scrutiny over the status of the virus in neighbouring Uganda and exposed lapses in Kenya’s border screening systems. The patient who died was able to pass through multiple airport temperature checks.

The World Health Organization (WHO) is working with Kenyan authorities to trace contacts and strengthen checks for travellers entering the country.

articles.title: MrBeast’s original logo sketch heads to auction with a $20,000 price estimate
articles.summary: A quick drawing made during a creative brainstorming session could soon fetch a five-figure sum.
articles.body: A quick drawing made during a creative brainstorming session could soon fetch a five-figure sum. The original pencil sketch behind MrBeast’s famous logo is heading to auction, with experts estimating its value at $20,000 or more. The artwork offers a rare glimpse into the early thinking behind one of YouTube’s most recognisable brands. However, there is an important detail for collectors to note: IGN has confirmed that Jimmy Donaldson, better known as MrBeast, is not involved in the sale. The auction puts the spotlight on how a simple design can become a valuable piece of internet history.MrBeast’s original logo sketch could fetch over $20,000The 8.5-by-11-inch pencil drawing will be offered through Heritage Auctions as part of its Fall Sports Catalog Auction, scheduled for October 23 to 25, 2026. The estimate of at least $20,000 reflects the creator’s enormous popularity and the cultural reach of his brand.The sketch dates back to around 2018, according to Heritage Auctions representatives, and reportedly took just 10 minutes to create during a brainstorming session. Today, the blue tiger logo appears across MrBeast’s online platforms, merchandise and chocolate brand.Yet the early artwork looks different from the familiar finished design. It shows the spotted big cat without the pink lightning bolt that later became part of the logo. The drawing also raises an amusing question about the animal itself.In an interview with Wired, Donaldson admitted that he had not spent much time thinking about the design.“even though that logo has probably been seen a hundred billion times, I actually put very little thought into it.”He also reflected on the childhood inspiration behind the image, saying, “When I was a little kid I just kind of designed a tiger, and here we are,” he said. “My name, my logo, probably should have had more thought behind it, I’ll admit it.”Donaldson has also acknowledged that he is unsure which big cat the logo represents. “I guess it’s kind of like a tiger,” he told Wired.Why MrBeast’s logo matters to collectorsThe auction highlights how internet culture is creating new kinds of collectables. Items linked to famous creators can carry value beyond their materials, especially when they document the beginnings of a widely recognised brand.MrBeast has built a huge audience through elaborate challenges, major cash prizes and philanthropic projects. His career has also expanded beyond YouTube, with his competition series Beast Games streaming on Prime Video. The show has been renewed for a third season.That success helps explain the interest in a seemingly modest pencil drawing. For collectors, the sketch offers a direct link to the early development of a brand seen by millions worldwide.Still, the $20,000 figure is an estimate, not a confirmed sale price.
